books.title: Firefighters
books.art_why: The book includes the 1666 Great Fire of London, an event before photographs existed.

pages.text: Introduction Can you hear the loud siren? It is the sound of firefighters rushing to fight a fire in their bright red fire truck. Firefighters put out fires and save people whose lives are in danger. They also help prevent fires from starting. They inspect buildings, and they teach people about fire safety.
pages.brief: A bright red fire truck with a loud siren races toward a fire. Firefighters rush to fight the fire and save people in danger. Others inspect a building and teach people about fire safety. The scene shows both rescue work and prevention work.

pages.text: What Makes Fire Burn Fires need both fuel and oxygen to burn. Some types of fuel are wood, oil, and coal. Oxygen is a gas in the air. The more fuel or oxygen there is, the hotter the fire will burn. Different kinds of fires are stopped in one of three different ways. One is to remove the fuel, and a second way is to smother the fire by removing its oxygen. A third way is to remove the fire’s heat with water. Do You Know? In our solar system, Earth is the only planet where fire can burn. Earth is the only planet with enough oxygen. Even a candle can’t burn without it.
pages.brief: A fire burns with wood, oil, and coal as fuel and oxygen from the air. A candle flame shows how oxygen feeds fire. Water, smothering, and removing fuel are shown as ways to stop fire. Earth is shown as the only planet with enough oxygen for fire.

pages.text: Types of Fires Firefighters put out house fires, factory fires, and forest fires. They must be prepared to fight many different kinds of fires and face other dangers, too.
pages.brief: Firefighters face a house fire, a factory fire, and a forest fire. They must be prepared to fight many different kinds of fires and face other dangers too. The scene shows firefighters standing ready in each of these three places.

pages.text: Firefighting Equipment Firefighters use many different tools to fight fires. Large hoses spray water or special foam on fires, and tall ladders reach high places. Axes chop holes in doors, roofs, and walls to reach places safely.
pages.brief: Firefighters use large hoses to spray water or special foam on a fire. Tall ladders reach high places. An axe chops a hole in a door, roof, or wall so firefighters can reach a place safely. The tools are shown with firefighters using them.

pages.text: Smoke masks and air tanks protect firefighters from smoke, and large fans remove smoke from rooms. Firefighters also use fire extinguishers to put out small fires.
pages.brief: A firefighter wears a smoke mask and air tank for protection from smoke. A large fan blows smoke out of a room. Another firefighter uses a fire extinguisher on a small fire. These tools help firefighters breathe and work safely inside a smoky building.

pages.text: Firefighting Machines Fire trucks are an important firefighting machine, and there are four main kinds. The most common, a pumper truck, carries long hoses and a pump to spray water a long way.
pages.brief: A pumper truck, the most common fire truck, carries long hoses and a pump. The pump sprays water a long way toward a fire. This firefighting machine is an important part of fighting fires. The scene focuses on this common fire truck.

pages.text: Other kinds of fire trucks include ladder trucks, tanker trucks, and rescue trucks. Ladder trucks carry ladders of many different sizes. Big ladder trucks have a ladder that can reach up to ten stories high.
pages.brief: A ladder truck carries ladders of many different sizes. On a big ladder truck, a long ladder can reach up to ten stories high. The scene shows the extended ladder reaching high into the air.

pages.text: Tanker trucks carry water to fight fires in places without water. Rescue trucks carry equipment to help rescue people who are trapped. There are other kinds of firefighting machines, too. Fireboats fight fires from the water by pumping water from under the fireboats and spraying it on the fire.
pages.brief: A tanker truck carries water to a place without water. A rescue truck carries equipment to help rescue people who are trapped. A fireboat pumps water from under itself and sprays it onto a fire from the water. These machines help in different firefighting situations.

pages.text: Helicopters dump water on fires in places that trucks cannot reach. Large planes help fight forest fires, too. Sometimes planes dump chemicals instead of water to slow the spread of a forest fire.
pages.brief: A helicopter dumps water on a fire in a place a truck cannot reach. A large plane helps fight a forest fire. Sometimes the plane dumps chemicals instead of water to slow the spread of the forest fire. The scene shows both aircraft above the fire.

pages.text: Becoming a Firefighter You must be at least eighteen years old to be a firefighter. Before you can become one, you must pass a written test and a fitness test. You must be in very good shape to fight fires. Firefighting school trains people to fight different kinds of fires. They also learn how to rescue people and how to treat them if they’re hurt.
pages.brief: A young person must be at least eighteen years old to become a firefighter. Before becoming one, they must pass a written test and a fitness test and be in very good shape. At firefighting school, trainees learn to fight different fires, rescue people, and treat people who are hurt.

pages.text: Conclusion Fire is useful, of course. Scientists think that people have been using it to cook for more than four hundred thousand years. Fires can keep us warm in the winter, and some forests need fire to stay healthy. At the same time, fire can be very dangerous to people and other living things. Every year, fire takes many lives and destroys large areas of forest.
pages.brief: Fire is useful: people have cooked with it for more than four hundred thousand years, and it keeps us warm in winter. Some forests need fire to stay healthy. Fire is also dangerous to people and other living things. Every year, fire takes lives and destroys large areas of forest.

pages.text: A Fierce Fire In 1666, the Great Fire of London destroyed most of the city. It also helped end an outbreak of the plague. The fire killed the rats and fleas that carried and spread the deadly illness. Fires also destroy thousands of buildings. Long ago, fires burned down entire cities because there was no way to stop them from spreading. Today, we have brave firefighters to put out fires and help keep us safe.
pages.brief: In 1666, the Great Fire of London destroyed most of the city. It also helped end an outbreak of the plague by killing the rats and fleas that spread the deadly illness. Long ago, fires burned entire cities because there was no way to stop them. Today, brave firefighters put out fires and help keep us safe.

books.title: Martin Luther King, Jr.
books.art_why: The book is about a named famous person, Martin Luther King Jr., so it is drawn rather than photographed.

pages.text: Martin Luther King, Jr.
pages.brief: A drawn portrait of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., a Black minister and civil rights leader, shown from the chest up in a dark suit and tie, with a calm, serious face. He stands against a plain, simple background, with nothing else in the scene.

pages.text: Growing Up in the South Each year in January, we celebrate Martin Luther King Day. We remember the life and work of a great leader. Who was he? Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was born on January 15, 1929. Where King grew up, white leaders made unfair laws. They took many rights away from Black people. They kept Black people and white people segregated, or apart.
pages.brief: A baby boy, Martin, born on January 15, 1929, held in a family home in the American South. Beside this, a Southern town street shows Black people and white people kept apart, using separate entrances under unfair local laws.

pages.text: Many places, such as schools, bathrooms, parks, and waiting rooms were segregated. The places for Black people were not as nice or clean as those for white people. Black people couldn’t live in white neighborhoods. They couldn’t marry a white person. As King grew up, he saw how these laws hurt Black people. He wanted to help. Martin Luther King Jr.
pages.brief: Separate public places in the segregated South: two school buildings, two bathroom doors, two park benches and two waiting rooms, the ones for Black people plainly older and less clean than the ones for white people. A young Martin watches and sees how unfair it is.

pages.text: King Goes to School King started college at the age of fifteen. He decided to become a minister. At school, King learned about a leader in India who used peaceful protest to help people. King decided to use peaceful protest, too. After King finished school, he and his wife moved to Alabama. He became a minister there. Coretta Scott King King’s wife was Coretta Scott King. She was an important leader. She started a center to teach people how to protest peacefully. She also helped make her husband’s birthday a holiday. She died in 2006.
pages.brief: Martin as a fifteen-year-old college student in a classroom, then as a young minister in a church. Beside him, his wife Coretta Scott King, an important leader who started a center teaching people to protest peacefully.

pages.text: Protest in Montgomery In 1954, the U.S. Supreme Court ended segregation in schools. Black people hoped this meant other places wouldn’t be segregated anymore. In 1955, a Black woman named Rosa Parks was riding a city bus in Montgomery. Black people had to sit at the back of the bus. They had to give up their seat to a white person if asked. Parks knew this was unfair. A white man asked for her seat. She didn’t move. The police arrested her. Martin Luther King Jr.
pages.brief: Rosa Parks, a Black woman, sits near the back of a Montgomery city bus in 1955. A white man stands over her asking for her seat, and she stays where she is. Police officers board the bus and arrest her.

pages.text: After Parks was arrested, Black people protested. They stopped riding segregated buses. They put King in charge of the protest.
pages.brief: Black people in Montgomery protest by staying off the segregated buses. Crowds walk and share rides instead of riding, and Martin Luther King Jr. stands before them, put in charge of the protest.

pages.text: A year later, buses were no longer segregated. The protest had worked. It showed that things could change. It helped King become a well-known leader. The Women of the Bus Protest Black women played an important part in the bus protest. Even before 1955, Black women were working for change in Montgomery. Women helped the protest keep going. They held meetings, planned carpools, and talked to protestors. Their work helped the protest succeed. Martin Luther King Jr.
pages.brief: A year later, Montgomery buses carry Black and white riders without segregation. Black women hold a meeting, plan carpools and talk with protestors, their work helping the protest succeed and King become a well-known leader.

pages.text: The Birmingham Protests White people who were angry about desegregation bombed King’s house. This didn’t stop King. In 1963, King started a protest in Birmingham, Alabama. Hundreds of people were arrested during the peaceful protest, including King. Black leaders raised money to get protestors out of jail. At another march the next month, police stopped the protestors. The police used fire hoses and attack dogs. Many of the protestors were hurt.
pages.brief: The 1963 Birmingham protest: hundreds of peaceful marchers, including King, are arrested. Police stop the marchers with fire hoses and attack dogs, and many protestors are hurt. King's house has been bombed, but he keeps going.

pages.text: When people across the country saw what happened to the protestors, they were angry. Black civil rights leaders and city leaders made a deal a week later. Birmingham would desegregate. People Who Inspired King Dr. Benjamin Mays (1894–1984) Mays was a minister and the president of the school King attended. He became a teacher to King. Howard Thurman (1899–1981) Thurman was a minister and King’s teacher at school. He taught King about peaceful protests. Mohandas Gandhi (1869–1948) Gandhi was a leader in India. His ideas about peaceful protest inspired King. Bayard Rustin (1912–1987) Rustin was a leader and King’s friend. He helped organize a famous march in Washington, D.C., in 1963. Martin Luther King Jr.
pages.brief: People across the country watch the news, angry at what happened to the Birmingham protestors. Beside them, drawn portraits of four people who inspired King: Benjamin Mays, Howard Thurman, Mohandas Gandhi and Bayard Rustin, each in plain view.

pages.text: The Work Continues King organized more marches and gave a famous speech. He called for equality for all people. The next year, the president of the United States made segregation against the law. The fight for civil rights was not over, though.
pages.brief: King stands at a podium before a huge crowd in Washington, D.C., giving a famous speech and calling for equality for all people. The President of the United States signs a law making segregation illegal, while the fight for civil rights continues.

pages.text: In 1965, King helped plan a march to protest how Black voters were treated in Alabama. King led the protestors. They didn’t get far before police attacked them. Three weeks later, the protestors marched again. This time, members of the U.S. Army sent by the president protected the protestors. Martin Luther King Jr.
pages.brief: In 1965 in Alabama, King leads protestors marching for Black voters' rights. Police attack them before they get far. Three weeks later the protestors march again, protected by members of the U.S. Army sent by the President.

pages.text: On August 6, 1965, the president signed the Voting Rights Act into law. It protected the right of all people of color to vote. The Right to Vote All Black people had the right to vote by 1920. State laws made it hard for them to vote, though. Black voters were forced to take unfair tests or pay money before they could vote. Sometimes white people attacked Black people if they tried to vote. Congress passed the Voting Rights Act to help fix these problems. It helped. Lawmakers changed the law in 2013. The change allowed state leaders to pass new voting laws. Some say the laws keep voting fair. Others say the laws make it harder for Black people and other people of color to vote.
pages.brief: On August 6, 1965, the President signs the Voting Rights Act into law. Nearby, Black voters are shown being forced to take unfair tests and pay money before voting, and white people attacking them, the problems the law was meant to fix.

pages.text: King’s Memorial In 1968, a white man shot and killed King in Tennessee. King died on April 4. People around the world were shocked and sad about his death. In 2011, a memorial for King opened in Washington, D.C. People from all over the world visit it and remember him. They carry on the work for justice and equality. Martin Luther King Jr.
pages.brief: A white man shoots and kills King in Tennessee in 1968, and people around the world are shocked and sad. In Washington, D.C., visitors from everywhere stand at the memorial that opened in 2011, remembering him and carrying on his work.

books.title: Blackbeard the Pirate
books.art_why: The book covers 1700s pirate events, so real photographs are impossible.

pages.text: The Man Behind the Stories Picture a pirate in your mind. Do you think of a cartoon pirate with a beard, an eye patch, and a parrot? Three hundred years ago, real pirates did sail the seas. One pirate had a name that scared everyone. He was known as Blackbeard.
pages.brief: An imagined pirate with a thick beard, an eye patch and a parrot stands on a ship’s deck, while behind him three hundred years ago real pirates sail on the open sea; one fierce pirate known as Blackbeard is shown as the most feared.

pages.text: Becoming Blackbeard Blackbeard’s real name was Edward Teach. He was born in England about 1680. When he was old enough, Teach learned to sail a ship. England was at war. Teach joined the crew of a ship that attacked enemy ships to help the English navy. Soon, he decided it would be better to join a pirate crew, instead! NORTH AMERICA West Indies CENTRAL AMERICA.
pages.brief: Young Edward Teach in England learns to sail; at sea he serves on a ship attacking enemy vessels for the English navy, then stands with a pirate crew, with a coastal map view of North America, the West Indies and Central America behind him.

pages.text: The leader of the pirate crew put Teach in charge of a pirate ship. They attacked so many other ships that everyone was afraid of them. Why did sailors become pirates? In those days, sailors worked very hard but made very little money. When a country was at war, any ship might be hired to attack and steal enemy ships. It was dangerous work. The hired sailors were paid a small reward for the ships or treasure they took. Pirates could attack any ship—even one from their own country! Pirates could keep all the ships and treasure for themselves!
pages.brief: Edward Teach, now in charge of a pirate ship, stands at the helm as his crew attacks another vessel; nearby, sailors work hard for little pay, and a hired ship attacks for a small reward, while pirates keep captured ships and treasure for themselves.

pages.text: One day, Teach and his pirate crew captured a large, fast, French ship. The pirate leader gave the ship to Teach as a reward. Teach added more cannons to make it a very dangerous ship. Then he gave his ship a new name—the Queen Anne’s Revenge. The Queen Anne’s Revenge and Teach soon became very famous. No ship wanted to see the fast ship and its black pirate flag chasing them. Edward Teach was now Blackbeard, the pirate. The Golden Age of Piracy During the 1700s, European countries set up new towns in the Caribbean and North and South America. English, French, Dutch, and Spanish cargo ships sailed back and forth. They were easy targets for pirates.
pages.brief: Teach receives a large, fast French ship, adds more cannons and renames it the Queen Anne’s Revenge; the black pirate flag flies as the fast ship chases another vessel, while European cargo ships sail between new towns in the Caribbean and the Americas.

pages.text: Blackbeard Ruled the Sea Blackbeard scared everyone who saw him. He was a huge man with a thick, braided, black beard. He stuck burning fuses in it. This made his beard look as if it was on fire.
pages.brief: A huge Blackbeard stands on a ship, his thick black beard braided and stuck with burning fuses so it looks as if it is on fire; sailors who see him look frightened as he rules the sea.

pages.text: Blackbeard soon had four fast ships and a crew of over 350 men. One time, his four ships sailed to Charleston, South Carolina. They robbed every ship sailing in or out of Charleston. Pirate’s Life for Me? How did Blackbeard get such a big crew? Pirates often shared treasure with their crews. Most sailors got little pay. If a pirate attacked their ship, sailors often chose to join the pirates! Some enslaved people joined the pirates as a way to escape slavery.
pages.brief: Blackbeard commands four fast ships and more than 350 men; off Charleston, South Carolina, his crews rob ships sailing in and out, while sailors with little pay and enslaved people choose to join the pirates, sharing in treasure.

pages.text: Sailing a large ship close to the land is hard to do. The water isn’t very deep. One day, Blackbeard and all of his men were sailing home with their treasure. Blackbeard sailed the Queen Anne’s Revenge too close to the land. His ship got stuck in the sand near a town on the coast called Beaufort. Blackbeard told his men to move the treasure onto the other ships. He dropped off many of his men on a nearby island. Then, Blackbeard sailed away, taking the loot with him. Had he wrecked his ship on purpose so he could keep the treasure for himself?
pages.brief: The Queen Anne’s Revenge runs too close to the shore near Beaufort and sticks in shallow sand; Blackbeard orders his men to move treasure to the other ships, leaves many men on a nearby island, then sails away with the loot.

pages.text: Virginia The Northern Outer Banks Islands Bath North Carolina Beaufort The Southern Outer Banks Islands South Carolina Charleston ATLANTIC OCEAN Georgia North Carolina Bath Florida Beaufort Beaufort Inlet.
pages.brief: A coastal map view shows the Atlantic Ocean beside the shores of Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia and Florida, with the Outer Banks islands, Beaufort Inlet, Charleston and Bath placed geographically along the coast.

pages.text: Blackbeard’s Last Fight For a time, it seemed that Blackbeard had stopped being a pirate. He got married and bought a house. People stopped worrying about him. Blackbeard soon went back to his old life, though. He went to sea in his last ship, the Adventure. Blackbeard began attacking other ships again.
pages.brief: Blackbeard marries and buys a house ashore, and people stop worrying about him; soon he returns to his old life, sails out on the sea in his last ship, the Adventure, and begins attacking other ships again.

pages.text: The governor of Virginia was tired of Blackbeard’s attacks. He sent a fighting ship called the Ranger to find and capture Blackbeard. One morning, the crew of the Ranger saw the Adventure near the island of Ocracoke.
pages.brief: The governor of Virginia, tired of Blackbeard’s attacks, sends a fighting ship called the Ranger to find and capture him; one morning the Ranger’s crew sees Blackbeard’s ship, the Adventure, near Ocracoke island on the water.

pages.text: The two ships fought, firing their cannons for many hours. In the heavy smoke from the cannon fight, the Ranger’s crew hid. They made it seem as though they had been killed. Blackbeard thought he had won, so he climbed onto the Ranger. The Ranger’s crew jumped out from their hiding places and the fight began again. Blackbeard fought hard, but the Ranger had too many men. He was shot five times before he finally died. The Ranger’s crew threw Blackbeard’s body into the sea.
pages.brief: The Adventure and the Ranger fire cannons for hours in heavy smoke; the Ranger’s crew hides as if killed, then jumps out when Blackbeard climbs aboard; he fights hard but is shot five times and his body is thrown into the sea.

pages.text: Blackbeard Sailed Into History Blackbeard’s true story may be behind the colorful pirates in many books and movies. The next time you hear a pirate story, remember one real pirate in history: Blackbeard!
pages.brief: On a ship deck, a colorful pirate figure from books and movies stands beside the real Blackbeard, a pirate from history, showing that his true story may lie behind many pirate tales that people hear and remember.

books.title: Kenya
books.art_why: Modern Kenya, its people, cities and wildlife all exist and can be photographed today.

pages.text: Kenya South Sudan Ethiopia Lake Turkana Uganda Somalia Kenya Lake Victoria Nairobi Tanzania Mombasa INDIAN OCEAN EUROPE ASIA AFRICA Where Is It? Kenya is a country in Africa. Part of the country is next to the Indian Ocean. Five different countries border Kenya to the north, south, east, and west.
pages.brief: Map of Africa with Kenya highlighted in red, showing the Indian Ocean along its coast and the five neighbouring countries—South Sudan, Ethiopia, Somalia, Uganda and Tanzania—pressing against its borders, with Nairobi and Mombasa marked inside.

pages.text: The capital of Kenya is Nairobi (nie-ROH-bee). More than three million people live there. The city has many businesses. Many different goods are made there. Nairobi has many hotels for people who visit Kenya. At one famous hotel, guests can eat breakfast with giraffes!
pages.brief: Busy Nairobi city street with tall offices, shops and hotels, people walking and traffic passing; nearby, a famous hotel garden where guests sit at a breakfast table while tall giraffes stretch their heads toward them.

pages.text: People More than forty-five million people live in Kenya. Kenya’s people belong to more than thirty different tribes. Kenyan people speak the language of their tribe. Most people also speak Swahili (swah-HEE-lee) or English. Swahili and English are the two main languages of Kenya.
pages.brief: Groups of Kenyan people of different tribes in colourful clothing standing together outdoors, some talking, a few holding schoolbooks, showing the many languages and peoples of the country.

pages.text: More and more people are moving to cities, but most people still live in the countryside. Many farm the land. They grow food to feed their families. They also grow crops to sell. Tea, coffee, corn, and wheat are some of the main crops. A worker spreads out coffee beans to dry at a factory in Kenya. Later, the beans can be ground up to make coffee.
pages.brief: A Kenyan worker in work clothes spreading dark coffee beans in wide rows on a drying rack outside a factory, with green countryside, farmland and a small family vegetable plot behind him.

pages.text: Kenya’s Landforms Lake Turkana Chalbi Desert Great Rift Valley Mount Kulai Merti Plateau Mount Elgon Kenya Winam Gulf Mount Kenya Lake Victoria Nairobi Loita Hills Yata Plateau Nyiri Desert Chyulu Range Mount Kilimanjaro INDIAN OCEAN Taita Hills Land Kenya has low land along the Indian Ocean. The land rises to become highlands in the west. The highlands include mountains and raised, flat areas.
pages.brief: Physical map of Kenya showing low coastal land by the Indian Ocean rising to western highlands, with Lake Turkana, Lake Victoria, the Chalbi and Nyiri deserts, Mount Kenya, Mount Elgon and Mount Kilimanjaro marked.

pages.text: The Great Rift Valley splits the highlands. This valley is a crack in the land that was made millions of years ago. It is 6,400 kilometers (3,977 mi.) long. The valley has deserts and lakes.
pages.brief: Wide view of the Great Rift Valley, a deep crack splitting the highlands, with steep cliff walls, flat valley floor, a lake and dry desert ground stretching far into the distance under open sky.

pages.text: Celebrations People from Kenya celebrate many special days. Great Britain ruled Kenya for many years. On December 12, 1963, Kenya became a free country. Every December 12, people celebrate with feasts, parades, and dancing.
pages.brief: December 12 celebration in a Kenyan town: people in bright clothes dancing, a parade moving along the street with flags, and families gathered around tables of food, everyone joyful.

pages.text: Kenya’s camel race festival starts in late August. It lasts for three days. People come from all over the world to race camels. At the festival, visitors also enjoy bike races, dancing, and local foods. They buy arts and crafts made by different tribes.
pages.brief: Camel race festival: riders racing camels fast across dusty open ground, crowds of visitors cheering, cyclists nearby, dancers performing, and market stalls selling crafts and local foods.

pages.text: Animals Kenya is famous for its wild animals. Some of them are very rare. Kenya has more than fifty parks and protected areas for animals. Every year, many people travel to Kenya to see these animals. Giraffes, zebras, and other grazing animals fill Kenya’s savannas. Lions and cheetahs live on the savannas, too.
pages.brief: Savanna in Kenya filled with grazing giraffes and zebras, dry grass and scattered acacia trees; in the distance a lion and a cheetah rest and watch the herds under a bright sky.

pages.text: Elephants, buffalo, and rhinos also live in Kenya. Crocodiles and hippos swim in its rivers and lakes. Kenya has more than a thousand kinds of birds. Wading birds live near lakes. Eagles and hawks glide through the air.
pages.brief: Kenyan wildlife scene: elephants, buffalo and rhinos on open ground, crocodiles and hippos in a river and lake, wading birds standing at the water's edge, and eagles and hawks gliding above.

pages.text: Conclusion Kenya has mountains and flat land. It has deserts, forests, and savannas. Many different tribes make up its people. Many rare animals are found there. Kenya is one of Earth’s treasures.
pages.brief: Sweeping view of Kenya's variety—snow-capped Mount Kenya, flat plains, desert, forest and savanna with grazing animals, and people of several tribes standing together in the foreground, all under one wide sky.

books.title: Magnetism
books.art_why: Magnetism is a real-world science topic with modern objects and experiments that can be photographed.

pages.text: Magnetism.
pages.brief: A plain cover-like image for a book about magnetism, with no people or action; the scene is simple and open, introducing the subject without a story moment and leaving only a calm empty background visible.

pages.text: Magnetism and Magnets.
pages.brief: A clear photograph of several magnets arranged on a plain surface, with nothing else in the scene; the image introduces the topic of magnetism and magnets and includes no people or action. The magnets sit still, and the background is simple so the objects are easy to see.

pages.text: Do You Know?
pages.brief: A simple, curious image with no people, set on a plain background, suggesting a question about magnetism; the scene is still and open, with nothing happening and no objects in action. It leaves space for the reader to wonder what comes next.

pages.text: Magnetic Field.
pages.brief: A magnet rests on a plain surface, and the area around it is shown as a magnetic field; no people are present, and the focus is only on the space around the magnet. The field is the main subject, with a simple background and no action.

pages.text: How Are Magnets Made?
pages.brief: A plain workshop-like image of iron and a strong magnet, suggesting how magnets are made; no people are shown, and the objects sit still on a simple surface. The scene focuses on the question of magnet making without showing a finished process.

pages.text: Some things, such as iron, become magnetized more easily than others. A piece of ordinary iron is placed inside a strong magnetic field. The magnetic force makes the iron atoms line up and spin in the same direction. This makes a new magnet. The more atoms that spin in the same direction, the stronger the magnet becomes. Sometimes if you drop a magnet, some of the atoms get knocked out of line, and the magnet gets weaker.
pages.brief: A piece of ordinary iron sits inside a strong magnetic field; its atoms are shown lining up and spinning in the same direction, making a new magnet. In a second view, a dropped magnet has some atoms knocked out of line, so the magnet is weaker.

pages.text: Try This Make your own magnet! You will need a large iron nail, a strong magnet, and several paper clips. 1. Hold the nail by one end and slide it across the magnet in one direction. Keep sliding it over and over. The magnet’s lines of force will start to line up the atoms in the nail. 2. After 20 to 30 times, touch the nail to the paper clips. Does the nail pick up the clips? How many can it pick up at once? Keep stroking the nail along the magnet to make the nail’s magnetic force stronger. See if you can pick up all the paper clips at once.
pages.brief: A large iron nail, a strong magnet, and several paper clips lie on a table. A hand slides the nail across the magnet in one direction, over and over, then touches the nail to the paper clips to see how many it can pick up at once.

pages.text: Magnetism and Electricity Magnetism and electricity are very closely related. Magnets can make electricity. And electricity creates magnetic fields. This is because both magnetism and electricity affect the way atoms spin.
pages.brief: Magnets and electric current are shown together, with atoms spinning to connect the two ideas; no people are present and the focus is on the relationship between magnetism and electricity. Magnets can make electricity, and electricity creates magnetic fields.

pages.text: All the electricity you use comes from machines called generators. Generators make electricity by spinning magnets around coils of wire. The magnetism creates an electric current in the wire. The difficult part is getting the magnets spinning. Power plants use running water, wind, or steam from burning fuel to turn the magnets.
pages.brief: A power plant generator is shown with magnets spinning around coils of wire, creating an electric current. Running water, wind, or steam from burning fuel turns the magnets, and no people are needed in the scene.

pages.text: Electricity can create special magnets called electromagnets. A wire is wrapped around a regular piece of iron. Then an electric current from a battery or outlet flows through the wire. The electric current makes a magnetic field. This magnetizes the iron. But the iron only stays magnetized as long as the electricity is on.
pages.brief: A wire is wrapped around a regular piece of iron, and an electric current from a battery or outlet flows through the wire. The current makes a magnetic field and magnetizes the iron, but the iron stays magnetized only while the electricity is on.

pages.text: Using Magnetism The earliest use of magnetism was the compass. A small, freely moving magnetic needle pointed to Earth’s magnetic north pole. This helped guide travelers and explorers. Modern travelers still use compasses. Electricity comes from spinning magnets inside generators. And electric motors work like generators in reverse. They use electric current to spin magnets. The magnets are attached to fans, cutting blades, or wheels. This is how fans, blenders, and remote-control cars work.
pages.brief: A small compass needle points toward Earth's magnetic north pole, guiding a traveler. Nearby, a generator spins magnets to make electricity, while an electric motor uses current to spin magnets attached to a fan, a blender, and a remote-control car.

pages.text: Magnets can also encode information, or store it in a special code. Hotel key cards and credit cards use strips of tiny magnets. The magnets are the size of grains of powder. There can be millions of magnets on one key card or credit card. Each tiny magnet points in its own direction. The different positions of the magnets create a code. Credit card and hotel door readers sense the tiny magnetic fields and read the code. Putting a credit card or key card near a powerful magnet can mess up or erase the code.
pages.brief: Hotel key cards and credit cards are shown with strips of tiny magnets the size of grains of powder. Millions of tiny magnets point in different directions to create a code, and a card reader senses their magnetic fields; a powerful magnet nearby can erase the code.

pages.text: Some high-speed trains run on electromagnets. The trains have powerful electromagnets on the bottom. The track also has powerful electromagnets. The two electromagnets face each other so that they repel each other. The magnetic force is so strong that it lifts the train off the track. The train floats above the track. It actually flies as it travels. This makes a fast, smooth ride.
pages.brief: A high-speed train floats above its track because powerful electromagnets on the train and on the track repel each other. The magnetic force lifts the train off the track so it flies along for a fast, smooth ride.

pages.text: 7 able to attract certain metals, such as iron magnetic field page 8 invisible shape of the lines of force around a magnet magnetic poles page 5 the ends of a magnet where the magnetic force flows in and out magnetism page 4 a force that pushes and pulls certain metals motors page 16 machines that turn electricity into motion using coils of wire to spin magnets repel page 6 force away.
pages.brief: Small science images illustrate a magnet attracting metal, the invisible lines of force around a magnet, the ends of a magnet, a motor turning electricity into motion, and two magnets repelling each other; no people appear and the scenes are simple.

books.title: Dragonflies!
books.art_why: Dragonflies are real animals that can be photographed.

pages.text: Amazing Dragonflies Bzzt! You’re walking by a pond when something zooms past your head. It’s bigger than a bumblebee, and it’s faster than a butterfly. It’s an amazing dragonfly!
pages.brief: A person walks beside a pond while a large dragonfly zooms past their head, wings spread wide. The dragonfly is shown larger than a bumblebee and quicker than a butterfly, with the pond and nearby plants behind them.

pages.text: What Are Dragonflies? Dragonflies are flying insects with long bodies and two pairs of wings. They come in every color of the rainbow. Some dragonflies have colorful stripes, and some even change color over time.
pages.brief: Several dragonflies with long bodies and two pairs of wings fly in the open air. Their bodies and wings show many rainbow colors, and some have colorful stripes. One dragonfly appears in two different color phases to show that some dragonflies change color over time.

pages.text: Young Dragonflies Dragonflies need water during every stage of their life cycle. Adults lay their eggs in water or on plants near water. The young dragonflies live in water for one or more years after they hatch.
pages.brief: An adult dragonfly hovers at the edge of a pond and lays eggs in the water and on plants growing near it. Below the surface, young dragonflies live underwater among the plants after they hatch.

pages.text: Young dragonflies look very different from adult dragonflies. They have gills inside their bodies, which allow them to breathe under the water. Dull green or brown coloring helps them hide from fish, frogs, and other hungry animals.
pages.brief: A young dragonfly rests underwater among green water plants, its dull green-brown body blending in. Nearby, a fish and a frog search for food, while the young dragonfly stays hidden with gills inside its body for breathing underwater.

pages.text: As dragonflies grow, their skin doesn’t grow with them. Instead, young dragonflies shed their entire outer layer every time they need to grow. When a young dragonfly is ready to become an adult, it crawls out of the water. The last layer of skin splits open, and the adult dragonfly climbs out.
pages.brief: A young dragonfly crawls out of a pond and climbs onto a plant stem. Its last outer layer splits open, and the adult dragonfly climbs out of the shed skin. Nearby, several discarded outer layers show how the young dragonfly shed skin as it grew.

pages.text: Super Sight Adult dragonflies have the largest eyes of any kind of insect. Each eye is made up of about thirty thousand tiny pieces. Dragonflies’ super eyesight, which allows them to see in almost all directions at once, helps them catch prey.
pages.brief: A close-up view of an adult dragonfly's head shows its enormous eyes filled with thousands of tiny facets. The dragonfly looks in almost every direction at once, watching small insect prey nearby as it prepares to catch them.

pages.text: Amazing Flight Dragonflies can speed up faster than the world’s fastest race cars! Dragonflies are among the world’s fastest flying insects. Large dragonflies reach speeds greater than 22 miles (36 km) per hour.
pages.brief: A large dragonfly streaks through the air beside a fast race car, its wings blurred with speed. The dragonfly pulls ahead, showing it can fly faster than the car and ranks among the world's fastest flying insects.

pages.text: Unlike most flying insects, dragonflies control each wing on its own. This skill lets them swoop and dive like fighter jets. They can fly forward, backward, and even upside down. Do You Know? Scientists study dragonfly flight to learn how to make better airplanes and helicopters.
pages.brief: A dragonfly swoops and dives through the air like a fighter jet, each of its four wings moving on its own. It flies forward, backward, and upside down. In the distance, an airplane and a helicopter suggest scientists studying dragonfly flight to build better aircraft.

pages.text: Amazing Hunters Adult dragonflies are high-speed flying hunters. They surprise mosquitoes and other small insects by attacking from behind and below. They kill their prey with a fast, powerful bite. Dragonflies often eat their catch without bothering to land.
pages.brief: An adult dragonfly hunts in midair, attacking a mosquito from behind and below with a fast, powerful bite. It catches and eats its small prey without landing, staying high above the ground as a speedy flying hunter.

pages.text: Dragonflies for Dinner Many animals like to eat dragonflies— birds, lizards, frogs, spiders, and even other dragonflies. Dragonflies’ flying skills help them avoid danger. Not many animals can catch these speedy insects. Humans eat dragonflies, too. In many parts of the world, dragonflies are a special treat. You can buy dragonflies on sticks for a snack.
pages.brief: A dragonfly flies through the air while a bird, a lizard, a frog, a spider, and another dragonfly watch, hoping to catch it. Nearby, a person holds a dragonfly on a stick as a snack, showing that humans eat dragonflies too.

pages.text: Swarms Dragonflies sometimes travel in huge groups, called swarms. They travel in swarms for food and to go south for the winter.
pages.brief: A huge swarm of dragonflies fills the sky, traveling together in a vast group. They fly south for the winter and move as a swarm in search of food, with many wings glittering across the open air.

pages.text: A Safe Place for Dragonflies In 1985, people in Japan created the world’s first dragonfly park. Today there are also dragonfly parks in Europe and the United States. Dragonflies are amazing creatures—and people all over the world are starting to realize it! Dragonflies Worldwide There are nearly three thousand kinds of dragonflies. They are found all around the world, in almost every kind of habitat. Check out your closest stream, pond, or lake. See if you can spot them for yourself!
pages.brief: In Japan, a dragonfly park features ponds and streams where many dragonflies fly among visitors. The park shows how people created a safe place for dragonflies, and the scene suggests dragonfly parks now exist in Europe and the United States and that dragonflies live in many habitats worldwide.

books.title: Eiffel Tower
books.art_why: The Eiffel Tower is a real place that exists today, with visitors, elevators, shops, and lights that can be photographed.

pages.text: A Famous Structure The Eiffel Tower is a structure that reaches up to the sky! The tower is famous. People around the world know about it. Almost seven million people visit the tower each year.
pages.brief: The Eiffel Tower rises high into the sky, its iron beams reaching upward. A large crowd of visitors stands around its base, looking up and walking near the tower. The scene is outdoors in daylight, showing the famous structure as a busy place people come to see.

pages.text: High and Mighty The Eiffel Tower is made of four long beams of metal. At the bottom, the beams are the four legs of the tower. The beams curve up and meet at the top. When the Eiffel Tower was built, it was the tallest structure in the world. With its big antenna, the Eiffel Tower is about twice as tall as the Washington Monument. Eiffel Tower: 324 meters (1,063 ft.) Washington Monument: 160 meters (525 ft.)
pages.brief: The Eiffel Tower’s four metal legs at the bottom curve upward to meet at the top, with a large antenna at the peak. Beside it, the Washington Monument stands much shorter, making the tower’s height clear.

pages.text: Paris FRANCE City on the Seine The Eiffel Tower is in Paris, which is the capital of France. The tower is much taller than other structures in Paris. It is at one end of a large park. The Seine (SEN) River flows next to the tower. Many museums, gardens, and ponds are nearby.
pages.brief: The Eiffel Tower stands at one end of a large park in Paris, much taller than the other structures around it. The Seine River flows beside the tower. Nearby are museums, gardens, and ponds, with the city spreading around this outdoor scene.

pages.text: A Tower of Strength Gustave Eiffel and three other men worked together on the idea for the Eiffel Tower. A contest was held to get ideas for a special structure for the 1889 World’s Fair. The men won the contest. It took many workers about two years to build the tower.
pages.brief: Gustave Eiffel and three other men stand together as the winning team for a contest to create a special structure for the 1889 World’s Fair. Around them, many workers build the Eiffel Tower, which took about two years to complete.

pages.text: The Eiffel Tower was built out of more than eighteen thousand pieces of iron. Iron is a type of metal. Mr. Eiffel wanted to prove that metal is as strong as stone.
pages.brief: More than eighteen thousand small pieces of iron are shown being assembled into the Eiffel Tower. Mr. Eiffel stands nearby, watching the metal parts come together. The scene shows iron as a strong metal, matching his wish to prove metal is as strong as stone.

pages.text: First, stone and cement were placed in the ground. Next, the small pieces of iron were put together to make the large beams. Then, workers put the beams on top of the stone and cement. The tower grew taller and taller.
pages.brief: Workers first place stone and cement in the ground. Then they put small pieces of iron together to make large beams. Next, workers lift the beams onto the stone and cement, and the Eiffel Tower grows taller and taller in the outdoor building site.

pages.text: Here to Stay Long ago, structures were not as tall as they are today. Many people thought Mr. Eiffel could not build such a tall tower. Other people thought the tower would be ugly. When the Eiffel Tower was finished, it was beautiful!
pages.brief: Mr. Eiffel stands beside the finished Eiffel Tower as people look up at it. Some people nearby had thought such a tall tower could not be built, and others had thought it would be ugly. Now the tower is complete and beautiful, rising above them.

pages.text: Mr. Eiffel wanted to make the tower useful to people so it would stay standing for many years. He put a science lab in the tower. Many people came to use the lab. Later, people used the tower to send radio and TV signals. The first French radio station with news and music began in 1921. It sent signals from the tower.
pages.brief: Inside the Eiffel Tower, a science lab is shown with people working. Mr. Eiffel wanted the tower to be useful so it would stay standing. Later, people use the tower to send radio and TV signals, and a French radio station begins sending news and music from it in 1921.

pages.text: Visiting the Tower Take a ride in a glass elevator to the top of the Eiffel Tower. The city of Paris looks amazing from that high! The second floor has shops, restaurants, and displays about how the tower was built. The first floor has a see-through floor. There is also ice-skating every winter.
pages.brief: Visitors ride a glass elevator up the Eiffel Tower, looking out at the city of Paris far below. On the second floor, people visit shops, restaurants, and displays about how the tower was built. On the first floor, people step on a see-through floor, and in winter they ice-skate there.

pages.text: The Eiffel Tower doesn’t always look the same. Workers paint it every seven years, and sometimes the color changes. The tower has been dark red, dark yellow, and brown at different times. It’s always huge and amazing!
pages.brief: Workers paint the Eiffel Tower while standing on its iron beams. The tower is shown in different colors at different times: dark red, dark yellow, and brown. Even as its color changes every seven years, the tower remains huge and amazing against the sky.

pages.text: Lighting Up the Sky In 2004, the Eiffel Tower’s lights were red for the Chinese New Year. In 2006, the lights were blue for another holiday. They were green and gold for a big sports contest in 2007. The tower had a special show of lights and fireworks to welcome the year 2000. Something fun is always happening at the tower!
pages.brief: At night, the Eiffel Tower glows with special lights. In 2004 it is red for Chinese New Year, in 2006 blue for another holiday, and in 2007 green and gold for a big sports contest. Fireworks and lights celebrate the year 2000 around the tower.

books.title: Adding It Up
books.art_why: Real farms, zoo animals, children, horses, cats and cubes can all be photographed.

pages.text: There are many ways to find the answers to addition problems. You can find answers by using: • cubes • your fingers • paper and pencil • mental math You are going to practice all of these ways to solve addition problems. Problem: On his farm, Mr. Patel raises chickens, turkeys, ducks, and geese. He has twenty-three birds in all. If he buys four ostriches, how many birds will he have on his farm?
pages.brief: Mr. Patel stands in a farmyard on his farm, surrounded by chickens, turkeys, ducks and geese. Twenty-three birds are gathered around him. Four ostriches wait nearby as the new birds he may buy and add to the farm.

pages.text: How many birds will Mr. Patel have if he buys four ostriches? Try using cubes to solve. 1. He has twenty-three birds now. Count twenty-three blue cubes to show this. How many tens do you have? How many ones? You have 2 tens and 3 ones. 2. He will buy four ostriches. Count four single orange cubes to show the ostriches. Now you can find the total number. You have 2 tens and 7 ones. You have twenty-seven cubes. Answer: Mr. Patel will have twenty-seven birds in all.
pages.brief: Blue cubes are grouped as two tens and three ones to show twenty-three birds. Four orange cubes sit separately for the ostriches. The blue and orange cubes are counted together, forming two tens and seven ones, twenty-seven cubes in all.

pages.text: You can use cubes in another way to find the total number of birds. 1. Just say the starting number, twenty-three. You don’t have to show twenty-three with cubes. 2. Lay out four cubes to show the four ostriches. 3. Use the cubes to count on from twenty-three. There will be twenty-seven birds in all.
pages.brief: Four orange cubes lie in a row on a table. A child’s hand points to them, ready to count on from twenty-three. The four cubes are counted forward one by one until the total reaches twenty-seven birds.

pages.text: You can also use your fingers to find the total number of birds. 1. Say the starting number, twenty-three. 2. You are going to add four to twenty-three. Use your fingers to count on from twenty-three. You can write an addition sentence to tell what you did. There will be twenty-seven birds in all. Riddle: When is it hard to count on using your fingers? Answer: If you are adding more than ten, you’ll run out of fingers! 23 + 14?
pages.brief: A child holds up fingers, counting on from twenty-three to add four. A pencil and paper lie nearby for writing an addition sentence. Nearby is a puzzled thought about adding fourteen, when fingers would not be enough.

pages.text: Problem: Isaac’s class is doing a project on reptiles. The children take a class trip to the Reptile House at their city’s zoo. They count forty-seven snakes and lizards. Then the class goes to the turtle pond. They count eight turtles. How many reptiles have the children seen in all? You have two numbers, or addends, 47 and 8. Try using cubes to find the sum. 1. Count out forty-seven blue cubes to show the snakes and the lizards. Make as many tens as you can. You have 4 tens and 7 ones.
pages.brief: Children from Isaac’s class visit the Reptile House at the city zoo and count forty-seven snakes and lizards. Later they stand by the turtle pond, counting eight turtles. Forty-seven blue cubes are grouped into four tens and seven ones.

pages.text: 2. Count out eight red cubes to show the eight turtles. 3. It’s easier to add from a ten. So, make another ten using the single blue cubes and the single red cubes. This is called bridging a ten. Answer: There are fifty-five reptiles at the zoo.
pages.brief: Eight red cubes stand for the eight turtles. The blue and red single cubes are rearranged to make another ten, bridging a ten. The grouped cubes now show fifty-five reptiles seen at the zoo in all.

pages.text: You can also count on your fingers to solve. 1. There are forty-seven snakes and lizards. Start with forty-seven. 2. You have to add eight turtles. First, add enough ones to get from forty-seven to fifty. It can help to find the total when you bridge a ten. 3. You have used three of the eight to make ten. Think: How many of the eight are left? 8 – 3 =? 8 – 3 = 5. There are five left. 4. Add the remaining five turtles. There are fifty-five reptiles.
pages.brief: A child counts on from forty-seven using fingers. Three fingers are used to reach fifty, leaving five of the eight turtles. The remaining five are added one by one, bringing the total to fifty-five reptiles.

pages.text: Problem: Owl Hill Ranch has six horses. Tall Pine Ranch has thirteen more horses than Owl Hill Ranch. How many horses are there at Tall Pine Ranch? This problem is different from the first two problems. Read it carefully! Be sure to answer the question that is asked.
pages.brief: Owl Hill Ranch has six horses standing in a pasture. Tall Pine Ranch has a larger herd, with thirteen more horses than Owl Hill. The two ranches are shown side by side as the question asks about Tall Pine’s herd.

pages.text: Cubes can help you picture the information and find out how many horses are at Tall Pine Ranch. 1. Start with what you know. There are six horses at Owl Hill Ranch. Use six green cubes to show those six horses. 2. Tall Pine Ranch has six horses plus thirteen more. Use six orange cubes to show those six horses. 3. Tall Pine Ranch has thirteen more horses than Owl Hill Ranch. Count thirteen more orange cubes to show all the Tall Pine Ranch horses.
pages.brief: Six green cubes show the six horses at Owl Hill Ranch. Six orange cubes show the same six horses at Tall Pine Ranch. Thirteen more orange cubes are counted out to show the extra horses at Tall Pine Ranch.

pages.text: 4. Now you need to add the two sets of orange cubes. Here is one way. You add thirteen orange cubes to that number. First, add the ten to the six. Then, add the remaining ones. You have six orange cubes. Adding is easier if you make a ten. You can also draw a picture to help you solve. Owl Hill Tall Pine +13 Answer: Tall Pine Ranch has nineteen horses.
pages.brief: The orange cubes are added: ten to the six, then the remaining ones, making a ten. A simple drawing shows Owl Hill Ranch and Tall Pine Ranch. The grouped orange cubes give nineteen horses at Tall Pine Ranch.

pages.text: Problem: Josh loves cats. He has cats on his wallpaper. He has cats on his bedspread. He has cat posters. He has one real cat, too! Josh also has a lot of books about cats. Josh loaned his friend Natalie nine of his books to read. Josh still has twenty-six cat books. How many cat books did he have before he loaned Natalie nine books? You know how many cat books Josh has now. You know how many he loaned Natalie. You don’t know the starting number. Think about this problem. Josh loaned nine books. He still has twenty-six books. To find the starting number, you need to add nine and twenty-six.
pages.brief: Josh stands in his bedroom amid cat wallpaper, a cat bedspread and cat posters, with one real cat and many cat books. His friend Natalie holds nine cat books she has borrowed. Josh still has twenty-six cat books.

pages.text: You can draw a picture and count the total. Josh has a total of thirty-five books. You also may be able to solve this problem in your head. Think: 26 + 9 can be hard to add. 26 + 10 is easier. 26 + 9 is one less than 26 + 10. Natalie Answer: Josh started out with thirty-five books.
pages.brief: Josh sits with a drawing of his cat books, counting a total of thirty-five. Natalie stands nearby with the nine books she borrowed. A thought shows twenty-six plus nine being compared with twenty-six plus ten.

pages.text: Problem: Owl Hill Ranch has six horses. Tall Pine Ranch has thirteen more horses than Owl Hill Ranch. How many horses do both ranches have in all? How is this problem different from Problem 3? Look back at page 9. In Problem 3, you needed to find out how many horses live at Tall Pine Ranch. For this problem, you need to find the total number of horses at both ranches.
pages.brief: Two ranch scenes are shown together: Owl Hill Ranch with six horses and Tall Pine Ranch with its larger herd. The question now asks for the total number of horses at both ranches, not just Tall Pine’s herd.

pages.text: Try using cubes to solve. Which group of cubes shows the horses at Owl Hill Ranch? Which group of cubes shows the horses at Tall Pine Ranch? Which group of cubes shows the total number of horses at both ranches? The addition sentence that shows what you did is 6 + 19 = 25. Check back at the cubes you chose. Did you choose correctly? or or or.
pages.brief: Three groups of cubes are laid out. One group has six green cubes for Owl Hill Ranch. Another has nineteen orange cubes for Tall Pine Ranch. The third combines them into twenty-five cubes for both ranches.

pages.text: Here are two other ways to solve the problem. Try solving 6 + 19 in your head. Think: 19 is about 20. There are twenty-five horses in all at both ranches. What pictures could you draw to solve this problem? Riddle: Can you think of a way that you could use your fingers to solve 6 + 19? Turn the page upside down for the answer! Answer: You could reverse the addends to get 19 + 6. Then count on from 19 with your fingers. Remember, you can add addends in any order. You’ll get the same total.
pages.brief: A child counts on from nineteen using fingers to add six, reversing the addends. Nearby, two ranch pastures hold twenty-five horses in all. A pencil and paper rest ready for drawing pictures that could solve the problem.

books.title: The Animal Data Files
books.art_why: Real zoo animals and children can be shown in photographs.

pages.text: Meet the Animals There are all kinds of animals at the County Zoo. The zoo has a Zoo Kids Club for children. Children in the club get to spend time at the zoo. They learn a lot about animals. Right now, they are helping to keep track of the zoo’s baby animals. From January to July, eight animal mothers had babies. Baby Animals Born at the County Zoo emu meerkat python tortoise armadillo swan camel opossum The emu is a giant bird that can’t fly. It can run fast, though. Emus are a lot like ostriches. The armadillo has bony plates of armor all over its body. This armor protects the armadillo from harm.
pages.brief: At the County Zoo, children in the Zoo Kids Club spend time with the animals and help keep track of eight baby animals born from January to July. A giant emu runs fast, and an armadillo shows bony armor plates covering its body.

pages.text: The meerkat is a long, skinny, furry animal. A meerkat often stands all the way up on its hind feet. Its tail helps it to balance. The Burmese python is one of the world’s largest snakes. This python can be longer than four adults lying head to foot. The Galapagos giant tortoise lives longer than almost any other animal. This tortoise might live for more than one hundred years. The swan has webbed feet to help it swim. This bird’s neck is longer than its body. The camel is used to living in very dry lands. It can go for days without drinking water. The opossum is a small, furry animal. It carries its newborn babies in a pouch.
pages.brief: At the zoo, a meerkat stands upright on its hind feet with its tail balancing it. A Burmese python stretches very long, a Galapagos giant tortoise rests nearby, a swan swims with webbed feet, a camel stands in dry land, and an opossum carries newborns in its pouch.

pages.text: Make a Tally The children use a tally to count the babies. Some of the babies were born. Others hatched from eggs. The children make a tally table to show their information. Tally Count means 1 Animal Mother Born or Hatched When Born or Hatched How Many opossum born January 8 python hatched February 20 emu hatched June 3 camel born April 3 armadillo born March 17 swan hatched June 10 Galapagos tortoise hatched May 11 meerkat born March.
pages.brief: Children make a tally to count baby animals, marking whether each baby was born or hatched and when. They sort the counts by animal mother, from the opossum and python to the emu, camel, armadillo, swan, tortoise, and meerkat.

pages.text: Close-Up: All in the Family How many animals are born or hatched from a mother at one time? It depends on the kind of animal! • A zebra gives birth to just one foal at a time. • A camel gives birth to just one calf at a time. • A hummingbird usually lays two eggs at a time. • A polar bear usually has two to four cubs. • One kind of armadillo usually has four babies that are exactly alike. • Some rabbits have eight babies. • A duck can lay as many as twelve eggs. • An alligator might lay forty or fifty eggs. Not all of them will hatch, though. • Some snakes lay as many as one hundred eggs! They won’t all hatch.
pages.brief: Different animal mothers appear with their young: a zebra with one foal, a camel with one calf, a hummingbird beside two eggs, a polar bear with cubs, an armadillo with four identical babies, rabbits with eight babies, a duck with many eggs, an alligator with eggs, and a snake with many eggs.

pages.text: Make a List The kids can use the data they have gathered in different ways. Data is information in the form of numbers. The data can show which babies were born or hatched first. The kids put the data in a list. Birthdays of the Zoo’s Animal Babies January 8—opossum’s babies born February 20—python’s eggs hatched March 8—meerkat’s babies born March 17—armadillo’s babies born April 3—camel’s baby born May 11—tortoise’s eggs hatched June 3—emu’s eggs hatched June 10—swan’s eggs hatched The list is arranged in time order. It shows the order in which the babies were born or hatched.
pages.brief: Children put the zoo babies’ birthdays in time order, arranging dates from the January opossum babies through the February python eggs, March meerkat and armadillo babies, April camel baby, May tortoise eggs, and June emu and swan eggs.

pages.text: Close-Up: Time to Hatch • Once an emu lays her eggs, the eggs take about 55 days to hatch. • A Galapagos tortoise’s eggs can take as long as 130 days to hatch. • A swan’s eggs hatch in about 35 days. • A python’s eggs hatch in about 60 days. Egg-Hatching Times for Other Animals hummingbird—11–16 days pigeon—about 17 days crane—about 30 days duck—about 30 days ostrich—about 40 days.
pages.brief: Eggs from an emu, Galapagos tortoise, swan, and python sit in different nests, each taking a different time to hatch. Nearby are eggs of a hummingbird, pigeon, crane, duck, and ostrich, showing other hatching times.

pages.text: List by Groups The data can show whether more bird babies, mammal babies, or reptile babies were born or hatched during this time. The kids sort their data by the class of animal. Classes are one way that scientists group animals. There are five classes of animals with backbones. They are fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. The zoo animal mothers belong to three of those five classes. The kids write the number of babies instead of showing tally marks. Numbers are easier than tally marks to read quickly. Birds Mammals Reptiles.
pages.brief: Children sort the zoo baby data into three animal classes: birds, mammals, and reptiles. They arrange pictures of the animal mothers and write numbers for each group, while the five vertebrate classes are shown: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals.

pages.text: Close-Up: Three Classes of Animals with Backbones Birds: Birds hatch from eggs. All birds have feathers. They are the only animals with feathers. All birds have wings, but some birds do not fly. Reptiles: Most reptiles hatch from eggs, but some are born live. Reptiles have scaly skin. Their body temperature changes with the outside temperature, so they can’t live in very cold places. Mammals: Nearly all mammals are born live, not hatched from eggs. Most mammals have fur or hair. Mammal mothers produce milk to feed their babies.
pages.brief: A bird with feathers and wings stands near a reptile with scaly skin, and a mammal mother feeds her baby milk. The bird hatched from an egg, the reptile has skin that changes with outside temperature, and the mammal has fur or hair.

pages.text: Make a Pictograph The data can show when the greatest number of babies were born or hatched. The kids re-sort data from page 5 to make a pictograph showing which month the most babies were born or hatched. A pictograph uses icons, or pictures, to stand for what is being counted. The key shows how many items each icon stands for. Animal Babies Born or Hatched Each Month To find the number for each month, read across a row. Skip-count by twos. You can also compare amounts by looking at how long each row is.
pages.brief: Children re-sort the baby animal data into a pictograph, placing small icons in rows for each month. They compare row lengths and skip-count by twos to see which month had the greatest number of babies born or hatched.

pages.text: Close-Up: Heart to Heart • Your heart beats about 90 times each minute. • A camel’s heart beats about 28 times a minute. • An elephant’s heart beats about 30 times a minute. • A gray whale’s heart beats only about 9 times a minute. • A cat’s heart beats about 120 times a minute. • A mouse’s heart beats about 500 times a minute. • A hummingbird’s heart beats as many as 1,200 times a minute!
pages.brief: A human heart is shown beside the hearts of a camel, elephant, gray whale, cat, mouse, and hummingbird. Their hearts are side by side, comparing how fast each beats, from the slow gray whale to the very fast hummingbird.

pages.text: Make a Bar Graph The kids present the same data another way. A bar graph uses bars instead of icons to show amounts. On a bar graph, you can find how many by looking at the number scale at the left of the graph. You don’t need to count. How to Read a Bar Graph for the Exact Number Animal Babies Born or Hatched Each Month • Read the labels to see what data the graph shows. • Find the top of each bar. • Look left to find the number at which the bar ends. Number of Babies Jan Feb Mar Apr May June Month Notice that the number scale starts at zero!
pages.brief: Children present the same baby animal data as a bar graph. Bars of different heights stand for each month, and the children read the top of each bar, look left to the scale, and find the amount without counting.

pages.text: Close-Up: Wing and Feather Facts • Penguins use their short, strong wings for swimming, not flying. • Bats are the only mammals with real wings. But their wings are covered with skin, not feathers. • The bones of flying birds are very light. In fact, all of a flying bird’s bones might weigh less than all of its feathers. • Feathers are made of keratin. This is what our hair and nails are made of. Number of Feathers Some Birds Have sparrow—about 3,500 bald eagle—about 7,000 swan—about 25,000.
pages.brief: A penguin swims with short, strong wings, and a bat flies on skin-covered wings. A flying bird shows very light bones and many feathers, and a close-up feather shows the keratin material shared with human hair and nails.

Then place the data in the list and tally table on the next two pages. • In what months were your friends born? • How many teeth have each of your friends lost?
