pages.brief: At a table, children write each friend’s name in the left column and use tallies in the right column to show how many teeth that friend has lost, collecting the tooth-loss data they gathered one by one.

books.title: Discovering Dinosaurs
books.art_why: Dinosaurs died out long before cameras, so their world and the fossil digs can only be drawn, not photographed.

pages.text: Finding Fossils How do we know dinosaurs lived on Earth? Scientists discover fossils in rocks all over the world. Studying fossils helps them learn about dinosaurs. They study what dinosaurs looked like, where they lived, and what they ate.
pages.brief: A rocky hillside where a scientist kneels with tools, uncovering fossil bones in stone. Around the wide landscape, other rock outcrops suggest fossils are found all over the world. The scientist looks closely at the bones, studying what the dinosaur looked like and how it lived.

pages.text: Fossils are the remains of plants or animals from long ago that have turned to stone. Scientists have found many different types of dinosaur fossils, including bones, footprints, teeth, nests, and eggs.
pages.brief: A close view of stone-like fossils resting on rock: a large bone, a tooth, a footprint shape, a nest of eggs and a few plant remains. The fossils look heavy and turned to stone, showing the many different types of dinosaur fossils scientists have found.

pages.text: These scientists are excavating, or carefully digging, fossils out of the ground. After recording information about the fossils, the scientists will wrap them to keep them safe. Then the scientists will take them to a museum. Scientists will study the fossils. They’ll examine the shape and color of the fossils. They’ll also consider where the fossils were discovered and how deep underground they were discovered.
pages.brief: Several scientists excavate fossils in a dig site, carefully loosening bones from the ground with small tools. Nearby, wrapped fossils are labelled and packed to keep them safe. A museum building waits in the distance where the fossils will be taken and studied.

pages.text: Scientists can sometimes fit bone fossils together to form a complete skeleton. Most dinosaurs had hundreds of bones, so it is difficult to find all of them. Scientists use other dinosaur skeletons to help them piece together the fossils and understand the missing bones.
pages.brief: In a bright workroom, scientists fit bone fossils together into a skeleton on a stand. Some bones are missing, so they compare other dinosaur skeletons to work out the shape. The nearly complete skeleton stretches across the room, with a few gaps still open.

pages.text: Learning from Fossils Although dinosaurs are extinct, the skeletons of other animals help scientists understand dinosaur skeletons. Some dinosaur bones may be bigger than those of animals alive today. However, many are still shaped the same.
pages.brief: A scientist stands beside a huge dinosaur skeleton and compares it with the skeleton of an animal alive today, such as an elephant. The dinosaur bones are bigger, but the scientist points out that many bones are shaped the same way.

pages.text: Many different types of dinosaurs roamed Earth. Scientists study fossils to learn how dinosaurs moved around. Some dinosaurs walked on two or four legs, and some used wings to fly.
pages.brief: A wide prehistoric scene shows several kinds of dinosaurs: one walking on two legs, one on four legs, and one lifting its wings to fly. They spread across the land, showing how differently dinosaurs moved around Earth.

pages.text: As dinosaurs moved around Earth, they left tracks behind. Scientists study fossil footprints to learn how fast or slow dinosaurs moved. Footprints also give clues about how big or small the dinosaur leaving the tracks might have been.
pages.brief: A trail of deep fossil footprints runs across flat ground. A scientist kneels beside the tracks, measuring the distance between them to work out how fast or slow the dinosaur moved, and how big the dinosaur may have been.

pages.text: Scientists study fossil teeth to learn about the diets of dinosaurs. Many dinosaurs grew new teeth to replace those they had worn down or lost. Some dinosaurs had razor-sharp teeth that helped them cut through meat or plants. Others had flat teeth that they used to grind their food.
pages.brief: Two dinosaur jaws rest side by side. One has long razor-sharp teeth, the other has flat grinding teeth. A scientist studies them closely, learning what each dinosaur ate, and notes rows of new teeth growing to replace worn ones.

pages.text: Scientists learn about dinosaur babies from fossil nests and eggs. Dinosaur eggs came in many different shapes and sizes. Some dinosaurs laid over twenty eggs at a time, while others laid only a few eggs. Like birds, some dinosaurs may have sat on their nests until their eggs hatched.
pages.brief: A fossil nest of eggs lies on the ground, the eggs in different shapes and sizes. Some nests hold many eggs, others only a few. A dinosaur sits low over its nest, like a bird, staying with the eggs until they hatch.

pages.text: Scientists find fossils of plants, fish, insects, and other animals in the same rocks as dinosaur fossils. These fossils help them learn what Earth was like when dinosaurs lived here. It’s also easier for scientists to find the age of the other fossils than dinosaur fossils. The other fossils are more complete than dinosaur fossils. They’re also found more often. Scientists can estimate the age of dinosaur fossils based on the age of the other fossils.
pages.brief: A scientist examines a slab of rock holding fossils of leaves, a fish, insects and small animals together with a dinosaur bone. The plant and animal fossils look more complete, helping the scientist judge what Earth was like and estimate the dinosaur's age.

pages.text: How Long Ago? Scientists can do tests to determine the age of fossils. Older fossils are found in rocks deep in the ground. Newer fossils are discovered in rocks closer to the surface. The oldest dinosaurs lived around 230 million years ago.
pages.brief: A cutaway view of layered ground shows fossils buried deep in lower rock and newer fossils in rock nearer the surface. A scientist takes samples and runs tests, working out the age of each fossil and how long ago the dinosaurs lived.

pages.text: Scientists aren’t sure how or why dinosaurs disappeared 65 million years ago. Studying dinosaur fossils helps scientists look for clues to understand what happened.
pages.brief: A scientist sits at a desk with dinosaur fossils and books, thinking about the mystery of why dinosaurs disappeared. Outside the window the land looks empty of dinosaurs. The fossils offer clues, but the answer is still unknown.

books.title: Jack-o'-Lanterns
books.art_why: The book mixes an old fable with historical carving traditions, so drawn scenes suit it.

pages.text: What Is a Jack-o’-Lantern? Carved pumpkins are called jack-o’- lanterns. Jack-o’-lanterns are used to decorate for Halloween. People started carving jack-o’-lanterns more than a hundred years ago. At first, people didn’t carve pumpkins. They used other vegetables instead.
pages.brief: Several carved pumpkins with cut faces glow as Halloween decorations. Beside them, older carved vegetables show what people used before pumpkins. The drawn scene hints at people decorating for Halloween more than a hundred years ago.

pages.text: An old fable from Ireland may tell how people began carving jack-o’-lanterns. The fable is about a man named Stingy Jack, who liked to play tricks on everyone. When he died, he was cursed to walk in darkness forever. He carved a turnip and put a light inside. His ghost was known as “Jack of the Lantern,” and then “Jack-o’-lantern.”
pages.brief: Mischievous Stingy Jack plays tricks on everyone, then his ghost walks in darkness forever. The ghost carries a carved turnip with a light inside. The fable shows how his ghost became known as Jack of the Lantern, then Jack-o’-lantern.

pages.text: Modern Jack-o’-Lanterns The Stingy Jack fable later became part of a night called All Hallows’ Eve. In Europe, people lit fires and dressed up to keep away ghosts.
pages.brief: In Europe, people light fires and dress in costumes to keep away ghosts during All Hallows’ Eve. The old Stingy Jack fable becomes part of that night. Drawn figures gather near the fire while ghostly shapes hover in the shadows.

pages.text: In Ireland and England, people carved scary faces on vegetables and placed a light inside. All Hallows’ Eve later became known as Halloween.
pages.brief: In Ireland and England, people carve scary faces into vegetables and place a light inside each one. All Hallows’ Eve later becomes Halloween. The drawn scene shows several lit vegetables with frightful faces glowing in the dark.

pages.text: When jack-o’-lantern carving was brought to the United States, people started using pumpkins. More than a billion pounds (more than 450 million kg) of pumpkins are grown in the United States each year.
pages.brief: In the United States, people begin using pumpkins for jack-o’-lanterns. A broad pumpkin field shows the huge crop grown each year—more than a billion pounds. Nearby, a carved pumpkin shows the new American tradition.

pages.text: Carving Jack-o’-Lanterns Carving pumpkins is fun for people of all ages. Smooth pumpkins work well for jack-o’-lanterns. Some people buy carving kits, while others carve without any help.
pages.brief: People of all ages enjoy carving pumpkins. Smooth pumpkins sit on a table with carving kits and simple tools. Some people use kits, while others carve without help. The scene shows young and old hands at work on jack-o’-lanterns together.

pages.text: First, with help from a parent, cut a hole in the top of the pumpkin to make a lid. Next, scoop out the inside flesh and seeds.
pages.brief: With help from a parent, a child cuts a hole in the top of a pumpkin to make a lid. Next, the child scoops out the inside flesh and seeds. The drawn scene shows the parent and child working together.

pages.text: Draw a design on the pumpkin, and then carve it carefully. After the pumpkin is carved, place a candle or other light inside. Finally, put the pumpkin lid back on top.
pages.brief: A design is drawn on the pumpkin, then carved carefully. A candle or other light is placed inside the carved pumpkin. Finally, the lid goes back on top. The drawn scene shows the drawing, carving, light, and lid.

pages.text: Jack-o’-Lantern Events Many cities have events to show off their carved pumpkins. In Hudson Valley, New York, jack-o’- lanterns make up a big display with spooky sounds and music. Pumpkins are used to make snakes, dinosaurs, and a dome carved with twinkling stars.
pages.brief: Many cities hold events to show off carved pumpkins. In Hudson Valley, New York, a big jack-o’-lantern display features spooky sounds and music. Carved pumpkins form snakes, dinosaurs, and a dome carved with twinkling stars. Visitors admire the glowing display.

pages.text: A huge display in Los Angeles, California, has pumpkin cars and dinosaurs. It also has pumpkin carvings of famous people. The artists carve their pumpkins at the event while people watch. Giant Jack-o’-Lantern An artist carves one of the largest jack-o’-lanterns ever recorded. The pumpkin was as heavy as a cow! The artist beat his own Guinness World Record for largest jack-o’- lantern, which he had earned five years earlier.
pages.brief: In Los Angeles, California, a huge display includes pumpkin cars, pumpkin dinosaurs, and carvings of famous people. Artists carve their pumpkins at the event while people watch. Nearby, an artist carves an enormous jack-o’-lantern as heavy as a cow, beating his own record.

pages.text: A town in New Hampshire broke a world record for the most lit jack-o’- lanterns. The town had thirty thousand jack-o’-lanterns lit at once! Halloween Under the Sea People even display carved pumpkins underwater. Some aquarium workers put carved pumpkins in large ocean tanks each autumn for visitors to enjoy.
pages.brief: A New Hampshire town breaks a world record with thirty thousand lit jack-o’-lanterns glowing at once. Elsewhere, aquarium workers place carved pumpkins in large ocean tanks each autumn. Visitors enjoy the underwater display of Halloween jack-o’-lanterns.

pages.text: The Tradition Continues Carving pumpkins into jack-o’-lanterns is a fun holiday activity. However they are carved, jack-o’-lanterns are a sure sign that Halloween is around the corner.
pages.brief: Finished jack-o’-lanterns glow in the dark in many different carved designs. Carving pumpkins into jack-o’-lanterns remains a fun holiday activity. However they are carved, the glowing faces are a sure sign that Halloween is around the corner.

books.title: New Year Celebrations
books.art_why: Illustrated scenes suit the book’s cultural celebrations and traditions.

pages.text: Introduction People around the world celebrate the New Year at different times of the year. They also celebrate the New Year in many different ways. Some people celebrate with parties. People have many different New Year traditions. Many people make New Year resolutions. A resolution is a promise to end a bad habit or begin a good one. It can be anything from cutting back on junk food to being a better friend.
pages.brief: People around the world celebrate the New Year in different ways and at different times. Some gather at parties and follow traditions. Others make New Year resolutions, promising to stop a bad habit or start a good one, such as eating less junk food or being a better friend.

pages.text: Africa Red Sea Eritrea Gulf of Aden Ethiopia EUROPE EUROPE AFRICA AFRICA Africa Enkutatash is the New Year celebration in the African countries of Ethiopia and Eritrea. It falls around September 11. The new year marks the end of the rainy season. People hold torches to look like the sun is shining. Families and friends eat together, drink coffee, and share gifts. Children often give daisies and make paintings. A girl collects flowers for the New Year in Ethiopia.
pages.brief: In Ethiopia, a girl gathers daisies for Enkutatash. Around her, family and friends share coffee and gifts, and people hold torches to make the rainy season’s end feel bright. The scene is set in eastern Africa near the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.

pages.text: North America Canada PACIFIC OCEAN ATLANTIC OCEAN United States NORTH NORTH AMERICA AMERICA Mexico Gulf of Mexico North America In the United States, around a million people come together on New Year’s Eve in New York City. They count down the seconds until midnight together. Then, the crowds cheer and celebrate. Many cities set off fireworks at midnight. A young girl and her father celebrate the New Year in New York City.
pages.brief: In New York City, a young girl and her father join a huge New Year’s Eve crowd. People count down the seconds until midnight, then cheer together. Fireworks light the sky over the city as many cities set them off at midnight. The scene shows North America and the United States.

pages.text: In the United States, special football games are played on New Year’s Day. Some people in Canada celebrate the New Year by jumping into freezing water. It is called a Polar Bear plunge. Do You Know? In the southern United States, people eat a dish made of rice and black- eyed peas. Some believe that if you enjoy simple foods on New Year’s Day, you might do well the rest of the year.
pages.brief: In the United States, football players compete in special New Year’s Day games. In Canada, people jump into freezing water for a Polar Bear plunge. In the southern United States, a dish of rice and black-eyed peas is served. Some believe eating simple foods on New Year’s Day may bring good fortune.

pages.text: Central and South America It’s good luck to eat twelve grapes on New Year’s Eve in Central and South America. Each grape stands for one month of the coming year. Cleaning your house before midnight so that good luck feels welcome is also a popular tradition. People sweep out the old to start the New Year fresh. CENTRAL AMERICA SOUTH AMERICA.
pages.brief: In Central and South America, people eat twelve grapes on New Year’s Eve, one for each month of the coming year. Before midnight, they clean their houses so good luck feels welcome. Sweeping out the old year helps them start fresh. The scene shows a home being cleaned and grapes ready to eat.

pages.text: At midnight, some people sweep in coins to bring wealth for the New Year. In many countries, people say goodbye to bad luck in another way. They throw water out of the window. Two-Faced! The month of January is named for the Roman god Janus. Janus was the god of doors, gateways, and beginnings. He is usually shown with two faces. One face looks backward at the old year. The other looks forward into the New Year.
pages.brief: At midnight, some people sweep coins into a home to bring wealth for the New Year. In many countries, people throw water out of a window to send bad luck away. The Roman god Janus, shown with two faces, looks back at the old year and forward into the New Year.

pages.text: Europe Scotland Denmark EUROPE EUROPE ASIA ASIA AFRICA AFRICA Greece Europe In Denmark, people smash old and broken dishes on the doorsteps of family and friends. This brings them good luck in the New Year.
pages.brief: In Denmark, people collect old and broken dishes and smash them on the doorsteps of family and friends. They believe this brings good luck in the New Year. The scene shows a doorstep piled with broken dishes in a European neighbourhood.

pages.text: In Greece, people bake a special cake with a coin hidden in it. If you get the slice with the coin, then you will have luck in the coming year! On New Year’s Eve, people in Scotland carry torches and swing balls of fire.
pages.brief: In Greece, people bake a special cake with a coin hidden inside. Whoever gets the slice with the coin will have luck in the coming year. In Scotland, people carry torches and swing balls of fire on New Year’s Eve. The scene shows the cake and the fire ceremony.

pages.text: Thailand Cambodia Philippines Southeast Asia In the Philippines, round things stand for coins and good luck. People celebrate the New Year by wearing clothes with polka dots. They also eat twelve different types of round fruit.
pages.brief: In the Philippines, round shapes stand for coins and good luck. People celebrate the New Year in clothes covered with polka dots and eat twelve different types of round fruit. The scene shows people wearing polka dots with bowls of round fruit nearby.

pages.text: In parts of Southeast Asia, people celebrate the New Year in late March or mid-April. It’s a very hot and dusty time of year—a time for water festivals. To prepare for the New Year, people clean statues of the Buddha with water. They save the water. Then, the water is poured onto people’s shoulders to bring them good luck. Water Fight! In Thailand, the water festival is called Songkran. It usually lasts from April 13 to 15. Parade floats spray crowds with water. Children chase one another with water blasters and water pails. It is very hot in Thailand on New Year’s Day. A water fight is the perfect way to celebrate!
pages.brief: In parts of Southeast Asia, the New Year comes in late March or mid-April, a hot and dusty time. People clean Buddha statues with water, save it, and pour it on shoulders for good luck. In Thailand’s Songkran festival, parade floats spray crowds, and children chase one another with water blasters and pails.

pages.text: Conclusion For some people, the New Year happens at a different time every year. The Islamic New Year is based on a calendar that follows the cycles of the Moon. The 365-day calendar is based on the time it takes for Earth to move around the Sun. The Chinese and Jewish New Years are based on both calendars.
pages.brief: For some people, the New Year happens at a different time every year. The Islamic New Year follows a calendar based on the cycles of the Moon. The 365-day calendar follows Earth’s journey around the Sun. The Chinese and Jewish New Years use both calendars. The scene shows calendars, the Moon, Earth, and the Sun.

pages.text: From fireworks to cleaning your house, people share many New Year’s traditions around the world. Most traditions help you begin the New Year with a fresh start and a fun celebration. How will you celebrate the New Year?
pages.brief: People around the world share many New Year’s traditions, from fireworks to cleaning the house. Most traditions help people begin the New Year with a fresh start and a fun celebration. The scene shows fireworks overhead and a clean, welcoming home as the old year ends.

books.title: Spain
books.art_why: The book includes maps and historical scenes from long ago, so drawn illustrations fit.

pages.text: Map of Spain BAY OF BISCAY FRANCE Pamplona ATLANTIC OCEAN Barcelona Madrid Balearic Islands (Spain) SPAIN PORTUGAL Valencia Córdoba Granada ME Strait of Gibraltar Canary Islands (Spain) Cueta (Spain) Melilla (Spain) MOROCCO Where Is It? Spain is a country in Europe. It lies south of a long mountain range. The country of France is on one side, and Portugal is on the other. A group of islands is also part of Spain. These islands sit off the coast, in the sea.
pages.brief: A map of Spain shows the country in Europe, south of a long mountain range. France is on one side and Portugal on the other. A group of Spanish islands sits off the coast in the sea. Nearby waters include the Bay of Biscay, Atlantic Ocean, and Strait of Gibraltar.

pages.text: Madrid is the capital of Spain. More than three million people live there. The palace is one of its biggest buildings. It used to be home to the Spanish king and queen and their family. Today, the family lives in a much smaller palace outside Madrid.
pages.brief: A large palace in Madrid is shown as one of the city's biggest buildings. The city is the capital of Spain, with more than three million people. The palace was once home to the Spanish king, queen, and their family. Today the family lives in a smaller palace outside Madrid.

pages.text: People About forty-eight million people live in Spain. Many people work at jobs in hotels and other places to take care of visitors. Other people grow olives or make cars and clothes.
pages.brief: About forty-eight million people live in Spain. Many people work in hotels and other places to take care of visitors. Other people grow olives or make cars and clothes. The picture shows Spanish people doing these different kinds of work.

pages.text: Spain belongs to a group of countries that work together to solve problems. People in Spain speak Spanish. Sometimes they also speak another language.
pages.brief: Spain belongs to a group of countries that work together to solve problems. People in Spain speak Spanish. Sometimes they also speak another language. The picture shows people in Spain talking together, using Spanish and sometimes another language.

pages.text: Spain’s Landforms Land Most of Spain has mountains and high flatlands. Beautiful beaches line its coasts. The Pyrenees (PEER-uh-neez) mountains in the north make a border between Spain and France.
pages.brief: Most of Spain has mountains and high flatlands. Beautiful beaches line its coasts. In the north, the Pyrenees mountains make a border between Spain and France. The picture shows Spain's landforms, with mountains, high flatlands, beaches, and the Pyrenees border.

pages.text: The mountains are 434 kilometers (270 mi.) long. They stretch from the Mediterranean Sea to the Atlantic Ocean. Different animals, such as the bearded vulture, live in the mountains.
pages.brief: The Pyrenees mountains are 434 kilometers long. They stretch from the Mediterranean Sea to the Atlantic Ocean. Different animals live in the mountains, such as the bearded vulture. The picture shows the long mountain range and a bearded vulture in the mountains.

pages.text: History Spain is very old. Long ago, people from different parts of the world moved there to live. The Romans built roads and bridges. Then, people from northern Africa arrived. They built a beautiful palace that still stands today.
pages.brief: Spain is very old. Long ago, people from different parts of the world moved there to live. The Romans built roads and bridges. Then people from northern Africa arrived and built a beautiful palace that still stands today. The picture shows these old roads, bridges, and palace.

pages.text: More than four hundred years ago, King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella ruled Spain. They made many important changes. They paid explorers like Christopher Columbus to sail on a ship and find riches for Spain. Today, the people of Spain choose leaders to rule the country. Spain still has a king, but he does not make the laws.
pages.brief: More than four hundred years ago, King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella ruled Spain. They made important changes and paid explorers like Christopher Columbus to sail on a ship and find riches for Spain. Today, the people choose leaders. Spain still has a king, but he does not make the laws.

pages.text: Celebrations Spanish people enjoy celebrating holidays. National Day is a festival on October 12 every year. It marks the day Spanish ships first arrived in the Americas. La Tomatina is a festival that happens every year in Spain. People throw tomatoes at one another and have fun.
pages.brief: Spanish people enjoy celebrating holidays. National Day is a festival on October 12 every year. It marks the day Spanish ships first arrived in the Americas. At La Tomatina, people throw tomatoes at one another and have fun. The picture shows these celebrations.

pages.text: Food Spanish food is tasty and has a huge range of flavors. Garlic and olive oil are used in many Spanish meals. Tapas, or small snacks, are eaten just before lunch and dinner.
pages.brief: Spanish food is tasty and has a huge range of flavors. Garlic and olive oil are used in many Spanish meals. Tapas, or small snacks, are eaten just before lunch and dinner. The picture shows Spanish food with garlic, olive oil, and small tapas snacks.

pages.text: Conclusion Spain has beautiful mountains and beaches. It’s an interesting country that makes our world a much more exciting place to live!
pages.brief: Spain has beautiful mountains and beaches. It is an interesting country that makes our world a much more exciting place to live. The picture shows Spain's mountains and beaches together, celebrating the country's interesting places.

books.title: Rainbows
books.art_why: Myth scenes, a historic scientist, and light diagrams suit drawn illustrations.

pages.text: Introduction When the Sun shines after it rains, run outside, and you may see a giant rainbow sweeping across the sky. Sometimes you may even spot small rainbows indoors when sunlight shines through a window.
pages.brief: After rain, a child runs outdoors beneath a bright sun while a broad rainbow arcs across the sky. Nearby inside a room, sunlight streams through a window and makes a small rainbow on the floor.

pages.text: Rainbows are illusions made by light. We can see them, but we can’t touch them or walk around them. Outdoor rainbows seem to move away when we go toward them. Rainbows appear when light shines through something clear like water. They are beautiful tricks of light, but science can explain the reasons behind the tricks.
pages.brief: A rainbow hangs in the sky like an untouchable illusion. A person walks toward it, but it seems to move farther away. Beside clear water, sunlight shines through and shows a bright band of colors.

pages.text: Where and When Rainbows Appear Look around the next time you see a rainbow—the Sun will be shining from behind you, and there will be rain in front of you. That is where you will see the rainbow.
pages.brief: A person stands with the Sun shining behind them and rain falling in front. Between the rain and the sunlight, a rainbow appears ahead in the sky, showing where the Sun and rain must be for it.

pages.text: Rainbows need water drops and sunshine to form. Rainbows most often appear in the morning or late afternoon, when the Sun is in the best places to create one. You might even see a double rainbow.
pages.brief: Water drops and soft rain fill a morning or late-afternoon sky over open land. A bright, low Sun shines as a rainbow forms, and above it a second, fainter double rainbow curves across the clouds.

pages.text: You may see rainbows in the mist of a waterfall, too. A splashing fountain can also create a small rainbow. Rainbows can even form under a bright moon. These are called moonbows.
pages.brief: A waterfall splashes mist into the air, and a rainbow glows in it. A fountain sprays water and makes another small rainbow. At night, bright moonlight shines through mist, forming a pale moonbow beneath the moon.

pages.text: We usually see a rainbow as a half circle. It actually forms a full circle, but from the ground we can only see the top half. Sometimes, a lucky airplane pilot may see the complete circle of a rainbow from the sky. Rainbows in Myths and Tales • Vikings said a rainbow bridge linked their gods to Earth. • In Ireland, people tell fairy tales about pots of gold hidden at the ends of rainbows and guarded by elves. • The Hindu god Indra is shown using a rainbow as an archer’s bow to shoot lightning arrows.
pages.brief: From the ground, a rainbow looks like a half circle, though it is really a full circle; high in the sky, an airplane pilot sees the complete ring. Below, Viking gods cross a rainbow bridge, an elf guards a pot of gold, and Indra draws a rainbow bow.

pages.text: How Rainbows Form Years ago, a French scientist decided to study rainbows. He used sunlight and a big globe of water to experiment. He found that to see a rainbow, a person must be looking at light from the right position.
pages.brief: A French scientist experiments with sunlight and a large globe of water. He studies how the light passes through the globe and finds that a person must stand in the right position to see a rainbow.

pages.text: Understanding how light travels helps explain rainbows. Think of running on land. Now imagine trying to run through knee-deep water. You will move more slowly through water because it is denser, or thicker, than air. In the same way, light moves faster through air than through water. Light bends when it moves between water and air, which is why a pencil sitting in a clear glass of water looks bent.
pages.brief: A runner wades slowly through knee-deep water, because water is denser and thicker than air. In the same way, light moves faster through air; a pencil in a clear glass of water looks bent where light bends.

pages.text: Outdoor rainbows form when water drops meet sunlight. The light bends as it enters each drop. The light then reflects, or bounces, off the back of each drop, like light off a mirror. The light bends again as it leaves the drop. Light bends and bounces in millions of water drops at once. This process makes all the colors of a rainbow. 1 Light bends as it enters the drop, splitting the sunlight into many colors. 2 Light reflects from the back of the drop. 3 Light bends again as it leaves the drop.
pages.brief: Sunlight enters a round water drop and bends, splitting into many colors. The light bounces off the back of the drop like a mirror, then bends again as it leaves. Millions of drops do this together, making a rainbow's colors.

pages.text: The Colors of the Rainbow Sunlight is made up of many colors. We can see them when water drops split the light into different colors. To see a rainbow, you have to be in the right place. Each water drop reflects colored light at a slightly different angle. We can only see red light shining from the drops at the rainbow’s top. Those drops are in the right place to shine the color red back at us. In the same way, we can only see violet shining from drops at the rainbow’s bottom.
pages.brief: Sunlight splits into many colors in water drops. At the top of the rainbow, drops shine red light toward a viewer; at the bottom, drops shine violet. Each drop sends colored light at a slightly different angle, so the viewer sees only some colors from each place.

pages.text: The colors of a rainbow always appear in the same order. The name ROY G. BIV can help you remember the seven main colors: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet. Make Your Own Rainbow 1. Fill a clear glass about three-quarters full of water. 2. Place the glass where sunlight can pass through it. 3. Hold a white piece of paper so the light shines through the water onto the paper. Move the paper around until a rainbow appears. 4. Use colored pencils to mark the different colors on the paper. How many can you see? What order are they in?
pages.brief: A clear glass three-quarters full of water sits in sunlight. A hand holds white paper so light passes through the water onto it, and a rainbow appears on the paper. Colored pencils lie nearby to mark the colors seen.

pages.text: Conclusion For a long time, rainbows have been featured in art and stories from all over the world. Most people find it hard not to stop and stare when a rainbow appears. Science explains how these colorful displays happen. Water drops bend, split, and reflect light, allowing us to see the many colors of a rainbow. Still, the beauty of a rainbow is a magical sight to see.
pages.brief: People stop and stare at a bright rainbow in the sky above a landscape. Around them are paintings and storybooks showing rainbows from art and tales, while water drops bend, split, and reflect sunlight to make the colorful display.

books.title: Great Zimbabwe
books.art_why: The ancient city and its past cannot be photographed, so drawn scenes fit.

pages.text: Great Zimbabwe.
pages.brief: A wide, quiet view of the ancient stone city of Great Zimbabwe, showing curved stone walls and ruins on open ground beneath a clear sky, with no people present, introducing the place named by the title.

pages.text: An Ancient City The ancient city of Great Zimbabwe was once rich and powerful. Now the city is empty. Its ruins give us some clues about what life was like there. However, there are still many mysteries about the people who once lived there.
pages.brief: The ancient city of Great Zimbabwe stands empty, with ruined stone walls and open ground. The scene suggests a place that was once rich and powerful, while its quiet ruins hint at clues and remaining mysteries about the people who lived there.

pages.text: Where Is It? The ruins of Great Zimbabwe are in the southeastern part of Zimbabwe. Zimbabwe is a country in southern Africa. It is north of the country of South Africa. It is west of Mozambique. Great Zimbabwe Great Zimbabwe AFRICA.
pages.brief: A drawn map of southern Africa shows the country of Zimbabwe in the continent, with South Africa to its south and Mozambique to its east. In the southeastern part of Zimbabwe, the ruins of Great Zimbabwe are shown.

pages.text: Who Built It? At first, European explorers were not sure who built Great Zimbabwe. However, experts can now prove that local people built the great city. Both works of art and the way that the walls were built help prove this fact. Most people think that the builders were a tribe called the Shona. The word Zimbabwe is thought to mean “stone houses” in the Shona language.
pages.brief: European explorers look at Great Zimbabwe with uncertainty, while local people, thought to be the Shona, are shown as the city’s builders. Curved stone walls and works of art provide proof, and the scene suggests the Shona meaning of Zimbabwe as stone houses.

pages.text: Building the Walls Builders used stone bricks to build the walls of Great Zimbabwe. First, they split huge rocks in the countryside to make bricks.
pages.brief: Builders in the countryside split huge rocks into stone bricks for Great Zimbabwe. They work among large natural stones, shaping pieces that will become bricks, with the open landscape around them showing where the rock was gathered.

pages.text: Then, they stacked the bricks to build high walls. They did not use anything to hold the stones together. However, the stones fit together tightly. The walls are well built. In some places, huge rocks form part of the walls. The walls of Great Zimbabwe are curved instead of straight.
pages.brief: Builders stack stone bricks into high walls at Great Zimbabwe. They use nothing to hold the stones together, yet the pieces fit tightly. In some places, huge rocks form part of the walls, and the walls curve instead of running straight.

pages.text: Three Areas The city has three main parts. The first is the Hill Complex, a large stone building on a hillside. This is the oldest area of the city. The kings of Great Zimbabwe may have lived here.
pages.brief: The Hill Complex is shown as a large stone building on a hillside in Great Zimbabwe. It is the oldest area of the city, and a king may have lived there, so the scene shows the stone structure rising above the slope.

pages.text: In the valley below, many smaller houses form the Valley Ruins. The houses were made of a mixture of clay and small rocks called daga. The people of the city lived in these houses. Across the valley is the Great Enclosure. Inside is a tall building in the shape of an oval. It is the largest ancient building in southern Africa and may have been a palace.
pages.brief: In the valley below, smaller houses made of clay and small rocks form the Valley Ruins, where the city’s people lived. Across the valley, the Great Enclosure contains a tall oval building, the largest ancient building in southern Africa, which may have been a palace.

pages.text: Great Zimbabwe Hill Complex Valley Ruins Great Enclosure The walls of Great Zimbabwe were: • 11 meters (36 ft.) high in some places—as tall as a three-story building • up to 6 meters (20 ft.) thick in some places • very smooth in some places.
pages.brief: A view of Great Zimbabwe shows the Hill Complex, Valley Ruins and Great Enclosure together, while the stone walls are shown as very tall and thick. Some walls reach the height of a three-story building, some are up to twenty feet thick, and some surfaces are very smooth.

pages.text: A Great City Great Zimbabwe was rich and powerful hundreds of years ago. The people raised crops and cattle. They also traded with other people from West Africa and the Middle East. They even traded with China, which is very far away from Great Zimbabwe.
pages.brief: The people of Great Zimbabwe raise crops and cattle in a rich, powerful city. They also trade with people from West Africa, the Middle East and faraway China, so the scene shows a busy exchange of goods in and around the city.

pages.text: However, after doing well for hundreds of years, the people left their city. They may have gone to find better farmland or better trade. Nobody knows for sure.
pages.brief: After many good years, the people leave Great Zimbabwe. Some may be seeking better farmland or better trade, and nobody knows for sure why they go. The stone city is left behind as the people move away.

pages.text: Mysteries Remain Scientists still have many questions about the ruins of Great Zimbabwe. For example, they do not know the purpose of some of its buildings. They also do not know why the people built the tall stone walls. Finally, there is the question of why the people left the city.
pages.brief: Scientists study the ruins of Great Zimbabwe and still have many questions. They do not know the purpose of some buildings or why the people built the tall stone walls, and they also wonder why the people left the city.

pages.text: The ruins of Great Zimbabwe have been damaged. People have stolen from the site. Wind, rain, and plants have caused problems. Laws protect the ruins, but more money and workers are needed to take care of the site. If the ruins are preserved, perhaps someday scientists can solve the mysteries of Great Zimbabwe.
pages.brief: The ruins of Great Zimbabwe show damage from wind, rain and plants, and some stones have been stolen from the site. Laws protect the ruins, but more money and workers are needed to care for them so scientists may someday solve the city’s mysteries.

books.title: Colosseum
books.art_why: Ancient Roman events and daily life are before photography existed.

pages.text: What Is the Colosseum? The Roman Colosseum was built almost two thousand years ago. It still stands in the center of Rome, the capital of Italy. The Colosseum is about the size of a modern sports stadium. Romans went to the Colosseum to watch different types of games. Men called gladiators fought each other in some games. In other games, men fought wild animals. Sometimes, wild animals were made to fight each other.
pages.brief: Built almost two thousand years ago, the Colosseum stands in central Rome, Italy, a huge arena about the size of a modern sports stadium. Inside, gladiators fight each other, men fight wild animals, and wild animals fight one another while Roman spectators watch.

pages.text: The Romans and Rome Rome once ruled a large empire. Romans fought many battles to defeat other countries and make their empire larger. One emperor of Rome built the Colosseum for the Roman people. He wanted them to enjoy games. He also wanted the building to stand for the power and glory of the Roman Empire. Roman Empire in the First Century ce BRITAIN ATLANTIC OCEAN MACEDONIA GAUL Rome SPAIN ASIA MINOR GREECE SYRIA ARABIA EGYPT AFRICA Roman Empire.
pages.brief: Roman soldiers fight battles to defeat other countries and make their empire larger. An emperor of Rome builds the Colosseum for the Roman people, wanting them to enjoy games and wanting the building to stand for the power and glory of the Roman Empire.

pages.text: Building the Colosseum First, large amounts of soil had to be removed from the ground to build the Colosseum. Then, workers began to build. Workers used wooden cranes to lift and move stones. Much of the building work was done by Jewish people who were enslaved after a war with the Romans. This modern crane is an example of the kind ancient Romans used to lift heavy stones.
pages.brief: Workers remove large amounts of soil from the ground. Others use a wooden crane to lift and move heavy stones for the Colosseum. Much of the building work is done by Jewish people who were enslaved after a war with the Romans. A modern crane is shown as an example of the ancient lifting machine.

pages.text: Important Parts The Colosseum was made in the shape of an oval. Seats rose in curved rows around an open space where the games took place. The Colosseum had four floors. Arches were built on three of the floors to help hold the weight of the stones above.
pages.brief: The Colosseum is a huge oval arena. Curved rows of seats rise around the open space where the games take place. The building has four floors, and arches on three of the floors help hold the weight of the stones above.

pages.text: Beneath the Colosseum were rooms where people and animals waited to come out to the stadium floor. A cover gave shade to the people watching the games. Wowser! Special lifts raised the gladiators and animals who waited underground up onto the floor of the Colosseum. The door to an animal’s cage and a trapdoor in the Colosseum’s floor opened at the same time.
pages.brief: Beneath the Colosseum floor, rooms hold people and animals waiting to come out. A cover gives shade to the people watching the games. A special lift raises a gladiator and an animal as an animal’s cage door and a trapdoor in the floor open at the same time.

pages.text: Violence and the Ancient Romans Violence was an important part of ancient Roman culture. Artwork showing violence appeared in many settings in Rome, including its monuments and public buildings. They served as reminders of Roman might and the power of the emperor. The Games The games at the Colosseum started in the morning. They lasted until darkness fell. In the morning, wild animal parades took place. Sometimes men would fight strong animals like lions and alligators. Other times, animals fought each other. Do You Know? Slavery in ancient Rome was not based on a person’s skin color or where they were from. Most people enslaved by the Romans were taken captive during wartime. Many Roman generals became rich by selling people into slavery after winning a battle.
pages.brief: Roman monuments and public buildings display artwork of violent scenes, reminders of Roman might and the emperor’s power. In the morning, wild animal parades take place; men fight lions and alligators, and animals fight each other. A Roman general becomes rich by selling captives into slavery after winning a battle.

pages.text: In the afternoon, gladiators fought battles. Gladiators were trained at a special school. Some gladiators had been taken in wars. Others were enslaved people. If they won enough fights, they might win their freedom. Some gladiators were freemen who chose to fight. They wanted glory.
pages.brief: In the afternoon, gladiators fight battles in the arena. At a special school, gladiators train; some were taken in wars, and others are enslaved people. A gladiator who wins enough fights may win his freedom, while a freeman chooses to fight for glory.

pages.text: Gladiators used many different types of weapons and armor. They had to make sure that the crowds watching them saw enough action. Powerful people, such as the emperor, sat in special ringside seats apart from everyone else.
pages.brief: Gladiators wear different types of armor and carry many kinds of weapons, making sure the crowd sees enough action. Powerful people, including the emperor, sit in special ringside seats, apart from everyone else, watching the fighters closely.

pages.text: The outer walls were filled with statues of famous Romans. 2 Gladiators and animals were led out from cages under the arena. 3 The wooden floor was covered with sand. 4 Free women and enslaved people watched from the very top. 5 People used eighty arches on the first floor to enter and exit the arena.
pages.brief: The outer walls are filled with statues of famous Romans. Gladiators and animals are led from cages under the arena, and the wooden floor is covered with sand. Free women and enslaved people watch from the very top, while people use eighty arches on the first floor to enter and exit.

pages.text: In the beginning, these games were very popular. However, over time people lost interest in the Colosseum. The building became a ruin. People began to take its stones away to make other buildings.
pages.brief: In the beginning, the games are very popular. Over time, people lose interest in the Colosseum, and the building becomes a ruin. People take away its stones to make other buildings, leaving broken walls behind.

pages.text: The Colosseum Today Today, the Colosseum is a ruin from ancient Rome. It is one of the most popular ancient buildings in the world.
pages.brief: Today the Colosseum stands as a ruin from ancient Rome. Visitors look at its broken stone walls and arches. It is one of the most popular ancient buildings in the world, and many people want to see it.

pages.text: Today, the Colosseum is an important part of Rome, as it was in the ancient past. The Colosseum has been chosen as one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. It is an important and lasting symbol of the ancient Roman Empire. People will be able to visit it for a long time to come.
pages.brief: The Colosseum is an important part of Rome today, as it was in the ancient past. It has been chosen as one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. It is an important and lasting symbol of the ancient Roman Empire, and people will visit it for a long time to come.

books.title: Why We Sleep
books.art_why: Keyword check suggests drawing, and the book includes historical ideas such as Aristotle’s belief about sleep.

pages.text: Introduction It feels great to curl up between soft sheets and slowly drift off into a sound sleep. Getting a good night’s sleep is important. We need sleep to function well. Like food and water, sleep helps keep us healthy and ready to go. Wowser! Did you know that people spend about a third of their lives asleep? That means someone who is seventy- five years old has spent twenty-five years snoozing!
pages.brief: A person lies curled up between soft sheets in a cozy bed, eyes closed, slowly drifting into a sound sleep. The bedroom is calm and restful, showing a person getting the good night’s sleep that helps keep the body healthy and ready to go.

pages.text: What Is Sleep? Falling asleep happens naturally and at regular times. It’s also easy to stop sleeping. A loud noise is often all that is needed to wake a sleeping person. So what is sleep? And what makes us fall asleep? A Greek thinker from long ago believed that eating made people sleep. That idea is not as strange as it sounds. Most people are ready for a nap after enjoying a big meal. Do You Know? The Greek thinker Aristotle believed that after people ate food, warm vapors went to their heads. The vapors then cooled and went to their hearts. This caused people to feel sleepy. While this is not true, how sleepy you feel does depend on the kind of food that you eat. Some foods cause a sleepy feeling. Others, like chocolate, have caffeine. Those foods can make you perk up instead of wind down. Aristotle.
pages.brief: A Greek thinker, Aristotle, sits and thinks about why people feel sleepy after eating. Warm vapors rise toward his head, then cool and move toward his heart. In another scene, a sleeping person stirs at a loud noise, while chocolate and other foods show that some foods wake people up instead of making them sleepy.

pages.text: Doctors learned more about sleep in modern times. They studied the brains of sleeping people. The studies showed that the brain does not really shut down during sleep—it just works differently. This discovery led to more studies on sleeping brains.
pages.brief: Doctors in modern times study the brain of a sleeping person. The sleeping person lies calmly while the doctors observe how the brain keeps working differently during sleep. Their discovery leads to more studies of sleeping brains.

pages.text: Doctors wanted to know just what causes changes in brain waves. They learned that the body makes a special substance as it uses energy. During the day, more and more of this substance travels to the brain. There, it slows down the parts of our bodies that are active when we are awake.
pages.brief: Doctors watch changes in brain waves. As a person uses energy during the day, a special substance builds up and travels to the brain. There it slows down the parts of the body that are active while the person is awake.

pages.text: The Need for ZZZs If our brain doesn’t shut off while we sleep, what does it do? It helps us learn by storing memories. The brain must organize new information we have learned. This happens while we sleep. It’s sort of like cleaning a closet. The brain sets things up to make it easier for us to remember and use what we’ve learned.
pages.brief: A sleeping person’s brain stays active, storing memories and organizing new information learned during the day. Beside the sleeper, a closet is being cleaned and arranged, showing how the brain sets things up so it is easier to remember and use what has been learned.

pages.text: Sleeping helps our body as well as our brain. When we are awake, we use energy. Body cells get worn down. When we sleep, new cells grow. Sleep helps keep the body from wearing down. For this reason, sleep is important to athletes. Whenever they train, they break down cells. They need enough rest to restore their body and make it stronger. This is also the reason that new babies sleep so much. Most babies double their birth weight in five months. Babies can only grow if there is more building-up activity than breaking-down activity.
pages.brief: A sleeping athlete rests after training while new cells grow to restore and strengthen the body. Nearby, a baby sleeps deeply; most babies double their birth weight in five months, and sleep gives them the building-up activity they need to grow.

pages.text: Sleep also helps us fight sickness and heal wounds. It strengthens the body’s cells that fight germs. During sleep, the body uses energy to heal instead of using it to play or work. That’s why doctors tell their sick patients to stay in bed and sleep. Sleep Problems There are a number of different sleep problems. Here are three of the best-known ones. • People with insomnia have a hard time falling asleep. Stress and worry may cause insomnia. Bad pain or sickness may make it very hard to sleep. • Narcolepsy is almost the opposite of insomnia. People with narcolepsy may suddenly fall asleep at any time. Some people’s muscles may become weak. This can cause them to fall to the ground and be unable to move. • Sleepwalking is more common in teenagers than adults. Sleepwalkers move about with their eyes open while asleep. They walk, talk, or even do chores. This usually lasts for less than ten minutes. While it is not harmful to wake a sleepwalker, it’s best to lead him or her back to bed.
pages.brief: A sick patient stays in bed to heal while a doctor advises rest. Nearby, one person lies awake with insomnia, another suddenly falls asleep with weak muscles, and a teenager sleepwalks with eyes open while asleep, doing chores before being led back to bed.

pages.text: Sleep Patterns Not all sleep is the same. Sleep goes through different stages. Doctors studied how people move and breathe when sleeping. They also looked at heart rates. They found that these things change as people sleep. Doctors learned that there are two types of sleep. One kind is rapid, or fast, eye movement (REM) sleep. The other kind is non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep. NREM sleep has three different stages. The first stage is short. It happens when people first feel sleepy and start to doze.
pages.brief: Doctors study a sleeping person’s movements, breathing, and heart rate as sleep changes. They identify two types of sleep: fast eye movement sleep and non-rapid eye movement sleep. NREM has three stages, and the first short stage begins when the person starts to doze.

pages.text: During stage 2 NREM, muscles don’t move much. Sleepers can no longer tell what is going on around them. This is the part of sleep when memories start to be made. Half or more than half of all sleep time is spent in stage 2 NREM sleep. During stage 3 NREM, sleepers begin to dream. The brain keeps storing memories. It is usually very hard to wake someone from this deep sleep. This stage lasts for nearly a quarter of sleep time.
pages.brief: A sleeper lies still in stage 2 NREM sleep, unable to tell what is going on around them as memories begin to form. In stage 3 NREM, the sleeper begins to dream while the brain keeps storing memories; this deep sleep is very hard to wake from and lasts nearly a quarter of sleep time.

pages.text: REM sleep is different from the other stages of sleep. During REM sleep, the sleeper’s closed eyes move quickly from side to side. It’s as if he or she is watching a ping-pong match. Yet the sleeper’s body is completely still. Muscles are frozen in place during REM sleep. Perhaps that is because people tend to have wild dreams then. Sweet (and Not So Sweet) Dreams We dream when we are in REM and deep sleep. We dream every night, although we don’t always remember our dreams. All dreams are like stories that play out in our mind. Not all of these stories are happy ones. Nightmares are scary dreams that can make sleepers wake up upset. Young children sometimes have bad nightmares called night terrors. Night terrors can cause them to scream and move about without being fully awake. For many years, people have wondered if dreams had secret meanings. Long ago, some people believed they were messages from the gods. Today, some people think that dreams come from our imagination. Others think dreams have hidden messages.
pages.brief: A sleeper’s closed eyes move quickly from side to side during REM sleep, as if watching a ping-pong match, while the body stays completely still. In another scene, a young child has a night terror, screaming and moving without being fully awake, and dream images swirl nearby.

pages.text: Getting a Good Night’s Rest Many things should happen when our tired head hits the pillow. When they don’t, we can have problems during the day. Too little sleep can make us grumpy. It can also cause us to make more mistakes. We may have a hard time solving problems. Our bodies have a hard time, too. Wounds take longer to heal. We might feel too hot or too cold.
pages.brief: A tired person’s head hits the pillow, but the night’s rest does not go well. The next day the person looks grumpy, makes mistakes, and has trouble solving problems. Their body also has a hard time, with wounds healing more slowly and feeling too hot or too cold.

pages.text: It is very important to have good sleep habits. Try to go to bed and wake up at the same time each day. This helps keep your body on schedule. You should also limit your screen time. Try not to watch television or use a computer, tablet, or smartphone right before bedtime. Also limit your activity before going to bed. Going for a walk is fine, but avoid a lot of exercise. Good sleep habits keep the body healthy and the mind sharp. Remember, if you don’t snooze, you just might lose!
pages.brief: A person follows good sleep habits: going to bed and waking at the same time each day, putting away television, computer, tablet, and smartphone before bedtime, and taking a calm walk instead of hard exercise. These habits keep the body healthy and the mind sharp.

books.title: Sled Dogs to the Rescue
books.art_why: The 1925 serum run is a historical event, so illustrated scenes suit the dramatic, snowy story.

pages.text: A Terrible Disease In January 1925, sled dog teams raced through Alaska in a blizzard to save children’s lives.
pages.brief: Sled dog teams race through deep snow in an Alaska blizzard, mushers urging the dogs forward on a desperate journey to save children’s lives. The dogs pull low sleds against wind and drifting snow, their heads low as they push forward.

pages.text: It started when a disease spread through a small town in Alaska called Nome. Two Native children died, and others got sick. The children needed medicine right away. The medicine that could save the children was in Anchorage, a great distance away.
pages.brief: In a small Alaska town, Native children lie sick while worried adults gather; two children have died. Far away in Anchorage, the medicine that could save the others waits, a great distance from Nome. The need is urgent.

pages.text: The medicine could be delivered part of the way by train. Even so, it was 674 miles (1,085 km) from the last train stop to Nome. Sled dogs were the best way to deliver the medicine through the snow, but the distance was too far for one team. A sled dog relay was the only hope.
pages.brief: At the last train stop, a train delivers medicine while sled dog teams wait in deep snow. The distance to Nome is 674 miles, too far for one team, so mushers prepare a relay. Dogs rest and mushers check harnesses.

pages.text: The Great Sled Dog Relay More than twenty teams, most led by Native people, would take part in the relay. Each musher would give the medicine to the next team along the way. When the medicine arrived by train, it was handed to the first team. The race was on. Alaska Nome Nenana sled dog route GULF OF ALASKA railroad A journey from the last train stop in Nenana to Nome would normally take twenty-five days by sled. The teams raced against time to deliver the medicine.
pages.brief: More than twenty sled dog teams, many led by Native mushers, line a snowy route across Alaska from Nenana to Nome. A train hands the medicine to the first team as the relay begins, racing against time. The journey normally takes twenty-five days by sled.

pages.text: The dogs battled through rough wilderness in the bitter cold, and some did not survive the journey. Often, the medicine had to be warmed by a fire to keep it from freezing.
pages.brief: Sled dogs and mushers push through rough, snowy wilderness in bitter cold; some dogs do not survive the journey. Beside a small fire, a musher warms the medicine so it will not freeze. The team fights drifting snow and icy wind.

pages.text: A famous musher named Leonhard Seppala and his lead dog, Togo, covered the most dangerous part of the run.
pages.brief: Leonhard Seppala, a famous musher, and his lead dog, Togo, lead a sled dog team over the most dangerous part of the run, through steep, icy wilderness. Togo runs at the front while Seppala guides the dogs across treacherous snow and ice.

pages.text: To save time, they raced over an area of frozen sea. The next day, they raced up snow-packed mountains. They covered 91 miles (146 km)—more than any other team.
pages.brief: To save time, Seppala’s team races across an area of frozen sea, then the next day climbs snow-packed mountains. They cover 91 miles, more than any other team. Dogs pull hard over ice and up steep snowy slopes.

pages.text: The Dogs Deliver The sled dog teams continued their difficult journey. Gunnar Kaasen, another musher, and his lead dog, Balto, left on the second to last leg in a terrible blizzard.
pages.brief: Gunnar Kaasen and his lead dog, Balto, leave on the second-to-last leg of the relay in a terrible blizzard, leading their sled dog team into wind and snow. The dogs push through deep drifts as the storm swirls around them.

pages.text: Balto led the team through the storm. At one point, a gust of wind flipped the sled over, and the medicine fell in a snowbank. Kaasen dug it out with frozen hands.
pages.brief: Balto leads the team through the storm. A gust of wind flips the sled over, and the medicine falls into a snowbank; Kaasen digs it out with frozen hands. Snow blows around the overturned sled and the struggling dogs.

pages.text: When Balto’s team arrived at the hand-off point, the next team was not ready to leave. Balto’s team continued on to Nome instead. Five and a half days after the relay began, Balto’s team delivered the medicine. The children were saved.
pages.brief: At the hand-off point, the next team is not ready, so Balto’s team continues on to Nome. Five and a half days after the relay began, they deliver the medicine, and the sick children are saved.

pages.text: After the Race After the race, Togo, Seppala, and their team went all over the United States, drawing large crowds.
pages.brief: After the race, Togo, Seppala, and their team travel all over the United States, drawing large crowds of people who come to see the famous sled dogs. The dogs stand beside Seppala as people gather around them.

pages.text: A statue of Balto was built in a city park. Balto and some of his teammates were in a dog show. They were not treated well and were kept in small cages. People gave money to bring the dogs to a zoo in Cleveland, Ohio, where they stayed for the rest of their lives. Balto is famous for his bravery. However, every sled dog on that journey helped save the sick children when there was little hope left.
pages.brief: A statue of Balto stands in a city park. Balto and some teammates are kept in small cages at a dog show; people give money to bring the dogs to a zoo in Cleveland, Ohio, where they stay for the rest of their lives. All the sled dogs are remembered for helping save the sick children.

books.title: Amazing Antarctica
books.art_why: Antarctica is a real continent that can be photographed.

pages.text: Amazing Antarctica.
pages.brief: A wide, sweeping view of Antarctica's icy continent, showing vast white ice and dark frozen sea stretching to the horizon under a pale sky, with no people or animals visible. The scene feels cold, remote, and amazing.

pages.text: North America 2 South America The Seventh Continent On it you can easily find six continents: Africa, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America. Now look at the bottom of the globe. There you will find continent number seven: Antarctica.
pages.brief: A globe seen from space with six continents visible across the upper half; the view turns toward the bottom of the globe, where Antarctica sits as continent number seven, surrounded by ocean and white ice.

pages.text: For a long time, no one knew Antarctica was there. It was located far from where anyone lived. People did not discover Antarctica until about two hundred years ago. Since then, we have learned a lot about Antarctica.
pages.brief: Long ago, people lived far from Antarctica and did not know it existed. An old sailing ship approaches a vast, distant icy land about two hundred years ago, with explorers looking toward the unknown continent across rough, cold seas.

pages.text: Antarctica is the coldest continent and has the strongest winds. Less rain and snow fall there than in any other continent. Antarctica is also home to some of the most amazing animals in the world.
pages.brief: Antarctica under fierce winds and blowing snow, the coldest continent, with very little falling rain or snow. In the icy landscape and nearby waters, some of the world's most amazing animals appear, adapted to the harsh conditions.

pages.text: Freezing Antarctica During the winter, Earth’s southern half is turned away from the Sun. For a couple of weeks in June and July— winter in Antarctica—the Sun never rises. For a period in December and January—summer in Antarctica—the Sun never sets. Its location makes the weather almost always cold, icy, and windy.
pages.brief: A view of Earth and the Sun in space, showing Antarctica's southern half tilted away from sunlight in winter, then facing the Sun in summer. Below, the icy continent is swept by cold wind under a dark or bright polar sky.

pages.text: The temperature in summer is usually just above 0°C (32°F). In winter, the temperature often drops below –18°C (0°F). The coldest known temperature on Earth was in Antarctica in July 1983. It was about –89°C (–128°F). This cold explains why thick sheets of ice cover much of Antarctica. In some places, Antarctica’s ice is more than 4 kilometers (2.5 mi.) thick.
pages.brief: Bitter cold grips Antarctica, where thick sheets of ice cover much of the land and reach more than four kilometers deep in places. Frost and blowing snow sweep across the vast white surface, showing the extreme temperatures of this frozen continent.

pages.text: With all that ice, it might seem surprising that Antarctica is also the driest continent. It gets less than 5 centimeters (2 in.) of rain and snow each year. Water covers most of Earth’s surface, but it is mostly salt water. Most of Earth’s fresh water is frozen in Antarctica’s ice. The ice has built up over many thousands of years. This happens because snow doesn’t melt completely during the summer.
pages.brief: Antarctica's dry, icy interior with only a thin dusting of snow and no rain, showing huge ancient ice sheets that hold most of Earth's fresh water. Layers of snow have built up over thousands of years because summer never melts it all.

pages.text: Life on and Around Antarctica The cold, icy, windy conditions have made Antarctica a dangerous place. Only low plants, such as moss, grow on the continent. No trees grow there. Antarctica has only one native insect.
pages.brief: A dangerous, windswept Antarctic scene with low moss clinging to rocky ground and no trees anywhere on the continent. The cold, icy, windy conditions make life hard; a single tiny native insect is shown near the moss.

pages.text: Almost all plant and animal life on Antarctica is found near the coasts or in the sea. Among the creatures that call Antarctica’s icy waters home are emperor penguins—the biggest penguin in the world. The leopard seal, a fierce predator of the penguin, also lives in the sea. Wowser! A male emperor penguin has a big job when it comes to a baby penguin. It stays on ice and holds an egg between its feet and body for two months. It does not eat and loses almost half of its weight. If the chick hatches before the mother returns, the father stays with the chick. Once the mother comes back, she feeds the chick. The father can finally go to the sea to eat.
pages.brief: Near Antarctica's coast and in its icy sea, emperor penguins and a leopard seal appear. A male emperor penguin balances an egg on his feet against his body, enduring two months without eating while the mother is away.

pages.text: A Playground for Scientists People around the world have worked hard to protect Antarctica’s animals and land. Many countries send scientists to Antarctica to do research. Some are there all year, even in winter. Others are only there in summer. Do You Know? No one country is in control of Antarctica. In 1961, many countries signed an agreement called a treaty. It makes sure no wars happen in Antarctica so scientists can study there.
pages.brief: Scientists from many countries work in Antarctica, some staying through the dark winter and others visiting only in summer. Nearby, people work to protect Antarctica's animals and land under an international agreement that keeps the continent peaceful for study.

pages.text: Many kinds of scientists come to Antarctica to work. Some study its animals. For example, some scientists study what penguins eat.
pages.brief: Scientists in cold-weather gear observe penguins near an Antarctic research area, studying the animals and learning what the penguins eat. The icy coast and sea surround the busy field team as they make their observations.

pages.text: Other scientists study Antarctica’s ice. They learn about how the ice has changed. Thousands of other people also visit Antarctica each year.
pages.brief: Other scientists examine Antarctica's ice, studying thick layers and learning how the ice has changed over time. Nearby, groups of visitors stand on the icy continent, part of the thousands of people who visit Antarctica each year.

pages.text: Conclusion Antarctica is one of the least-known lands in the world. The cold, ice, and rough seas make it a difficult place to explore and study. However, it’s a place of amazing beauty and an important place to protect.
pages.brief: A dramatic view of Antarctica's remote icy beauty, with rough seas crashing against towering ice and vast white landscapes stretching far away. The continent remains one of the least-known lands, difficult to explore and study, yet clearly important to protect.

books.title: The Seed Sowers
books.art_why: Real animals, plants, and natural processes are shown in nature.

pages.text: The Seed Sowers.
pages.brief: A close view of a single seed, centered as the only subject on the page, with no people or animals present. The seed rests alone, representing the book’s title and theme of seeds being spread and planted.

pages.text: Finned Farmers Fall sunlight peeks through the trees and shines on a stream below. A breeze scatters leaves and fruit across the water. Suddenly, a fish breaks the surface to feed. The fish snaps up a floating piece of fruit. Then it disappears beneath the water and swims downstream. It’s easy to see how the trees help the fish, but the fish also helps the trees. By eating the fruit, the fish is spreading the tree’s seeds. It’s one of nature’s seed sowers.
pages.brief: Sunlight filters through trees onto a stream. A breeze scatters leaves and fruit across the water. A fish breaks the surface and snaps up a floating piece of fruit, then disappears beneath the water and swims downstream.

pages.text: Room to Grow Seed sowers are important to plants. Seeds are the way most plants reproduce. All seeds need the same things to sprout and grow. Plants must get enough sunlight, water, and nutrients to thrive. People who grow crops know this. They do their best to make sure their plants get those things. Farmers spread seeds so plants don’t have to compete for what they need. They plant the seeds far enough apart for each plant to thrive.
pages.brief: Farmers spread seeds across the ground, spacing them far apart so each plant has room. Young crop plants stand with sunlight, water, and soil nutrients reaching them, showing what plants need to sprout and thrive.

pages.text: Trees and other wild plants need room to grow, too. They can’t depend on farmers to spread their seeds. Instead, wild plants depend on nature to do the job. Some seeds are blown by the wind, while others float away on water. Some seeds are carried off by animals, often on purpose. Animals may hide seeds to eat later, or they may take seeds to feed to their young. Some animals spread seeds without even trying. Many seeds sprout far and wide thanks to animal seed sowers. The word zoo refers to animals. It’s part of the word zoochory. Zoochory is the scientific name for the process of animals spreading seeds.
pages.brief: Wild plants grow without farmers. Wind blows some seeds through the air, others float away on water, and animals carry seeds off—some hidden to eat later, some taken to feed young. Many seeds sprout far and wide thanks to these animal seed sowers.

pages.text: Tasty, Pretty, and Sticky Wild plants have many ways to get animals to carry their seeds. Some seeds just taste good. Animals seek them out to eat. For example, bears and deer love the taste of acorns. Even if a seed doesn’t taste good to an animal, its fruit might. Papaya seeds taste peppery. The fruit around the seeds, however, is sweet. Animals that eat the fruit sometimes eat the seeds, too.
pages.brief: A bear and a deer seek out acorns because they taste good. Nearby, a papaya is split open to show peppery seeds surrounded by sweet fruit, and an animal eats the fruit along with some seeds.

pages.text: Many plants make fruit or seeds that are easy for animals to spot. Some animals see certain colors better than others. Blackbirds, for example, are attracted to red fruits and berries. Seeds on the ground have a special trick for getting around. Many, such as burrs, have small hooks or teeth. The hooks attach to the hair or fur of passing animals. If you take a dog for a walk through a field in autumn, it may come home covered in burrs. Foxtail grass grows in the western United States. It has spiked seeds that spread by burrowing into the soil. However, the seeds can also spread by hitching a ride on an animal’s fur. The seeds may enter the animal’s ears, mouth, or nose and dig deep inside its body. This can lead to a bad infection or worse if not treated.
pages.brief: A blackbird spots bright red fruits and berries. A dog walks through a field in autumn and comes home covered in burrs whose small hooks cling to its fur. Foxtail grass grows in the western United States, its spiked seeds able to burrow into soil or hitch a ride on an animal.

pages.text: All Kinds of Seed Sowers Some animals seem to be made for seed sowing. Gray squirrels, for example, gather acorns and other large seeds to store for winter. They run through woods or fields and bury their food stash along the way. Squirrels don’t always remember where they put their stash, however. Come springtime, those forgotten seeds sprout, and new trees begin to grow.
pages.brief: Gray squirrels gather acorns and other large seeds for winter. They run through woods and fields, burying their food stash along the way. Some buried seeds are forgotten; in springtime those seeds sprout and new trees begin to grow.

pages.text: Insects are also seed sowers. Ants drag seeds to their underground nests. They are only interested in eating the tasty, fatty part of seeds. They leave the rest to sprout and bloom later. Ants till the ground, too. They dig up soil as they hunt for seeds. This improves growing conditions for the seeds they leave.
pages.brief: Ants drag seeds across the ground and down into their underground nests. They eat only the tasty, fatty part of the seeds and leave the rest to sprout and bloom later. As they dig up soil hunting for seeds, they improve growing conditions.

pages.text: Reptiles are seed sowers as well. Giant Galapagos tortoises are amazing seed- spreading machines. They can eat, move, and poop the seeds of more than forty- five plant species. They spread seeds over great distances. Colombia’s green common iguanas do their fair share, too. Iguanas crawl over plants while eating their leaves. Seeds stick to their snout and to a flap of skin hanging from their neck called a dewlap. Later the seeds drop to the ground far from the parent plant.
pages.brief: A giant Galapagos tortoise walks slowly, eating plants and pooping seeds over great distances. A green common iguana crawls over leafy plants while eating, with seeds sticking to its snout and the flap of skin under its neck before dropping to the ground.

pages.text: Nature’s “flying farmers” are important seed spreaders. In tropical areas, fruit bats are attracted to the smells of mangos and bananas. They feast on these fruits and spread their seeds far and wide. Toucans spread seeds by throwing up! They have large beaks made for cracking the tasty, fatty shells of wild nutmegs. Toucans eat the shells and spit up any seeds they accidentally swallow. Fruit bats are great seed sowers. Scientists are studying how fruit bats can help spread seeds to places where forests have burned or been cut down. Feeding boxes that attract bats are filled with fresh fruit and placed in those areas. Bats eat the fruit and then poop the seeds, providing a low-cost way to get forests growing again!
pages.brief: Fruit bats feast on ripe mangos and bananas in a tropical area, spreading seeds far and wide. A toucan cracks the fatty shells of wild nutmegs and spits up swallowed seeds. Scientists place feeding boxes filled with fresh fruit where forests have burned, attracting bats that poop seeds and help forests regrow.

pages.text: The Scoop on Poop You may wonder how a seed that is eaten can later grow. The answer is simple— animal poop. Sometimes passing through an animal’s body helps seeds grow faster. One example is the kerer ū (KAIR-uh- roo) bird of New Zealand. The bird’s poop helps native berry plants grow. First, the bird swallows the large berries of the karaka (KAH-rah-kuh) tree. Then its stomach juices weaken the hard coating of the seeds inside the berries. By the time the bird poops the seeds, their hard shells are gone, and they are ready to grow. Plus, they are sitting in a damp pile of poop, which acts like a rich fertilizer!
pages.brief: A kererū bird in New Zealand swallows large karaka berries. Its stomach juices weaken the hard seed coatings, and by the time it poops the seeds, their shells are gone. The seeds sit in a damp pile of poop that acts like rich fertilizer, ready to grow.

pages.text: Some large animals are great seed sowers because of how much they eat. Elephants have big appetites and poop a lot. They can eat a meal and poop the seeds up to 65 kilometers (40 mi.) away. Where there is elephant poop, there are also dung beetles. The beetles shape bits of poop into balls, roll them away, and lay eggs inside. Within fifteen minutes, a swarm of beetles can cart away half a liter (1 pt.) of poop! The seeds from the elephant’s meal are spread out even more, with help from the beetles.
