pages.brief: A big elephant eats a meal and later poops seeds up to 65 kilometers away. Dung beetles gather around the poop, shape bits into balls, roll them away, and lay eggs inside. A swarm of beetles can cart away half a liter of poop within fifteen minutes.

pages.text: Thanks to the Seed Sowers From elephants to beetles and birds to bats, nature gives us a wealth of seed sowers. They spread seeds near and far, each in their own way. Thanks to them, the world keeps producing healthy environments where both plants and animals can thrive.
pages.brief: Elephants, beetles, birds, and bats appear together in a wide natural landscape, each spreading seeds in its own way. Seeds are scattered near and far, and healthy environments flourish with plants and animals thriving together.

books.title: Dinosaurs
books.art_why: Dinosaurs are prehistoric and no photographs exist; scenes must be reconstructed from fossils.

pages.text: The World of Dinosaurs Imagine that you’ve been sent back in time 230 million years. The world looks very different from the one you know. All the land on Earth is one giant continent. Shallow seas cover parts of the ground. The weather is warm, even near the poles. In the shadow of an enormous plant, you hear a noise. Something large is hiding there.
pages.brief: A lone time traveler stands in a warm prehistoric landscape 230 million years ago. All land forms one giant continent, with shallow seas covering parts of the ground. Near the poles the air is warm. In the shadow of an enormous plant, a large creature hides, partly visible.

pages.text: You have arrived in the time of the dinosaurs. You are probably familiar with dinosaurs from books and movies. These animals were just one part of an entire ancient world. The age of dinosaurs lasted for about 180 million years. Earth changed a lot during that time. The continents split apart, and the first flowering plants grew.
pages.brief: Dinosaurs roam an ancient world beside other creatures. Across a changing landscape, continents begin to split apart. Small flowering plants grow among older vegetation. The scene suggests a long age of dinosaurs stretching over millions of years, with different environments and life forms sharing the land.

pages.text: Some kinds of dinosaurs died out, and new ones appeared. Like today’s world, the world of the dinosaurs was a changing place.
pages.brief: Against a broad prehistoric landscape, some dinosaurs fade from view while new kinds appear in their place. The land and plant life around them shift over time, showing that the world of the dinosaurs was always changing, much like the natural world today.

pages.text: Meet the Dinosaurs Dinosaurs were a kind of reptile that is now extinct. Dinosaurs stood up off the ground, while other reptiles crawled. They had large eyes and could probably see color. Many scientists think that dinosaurs were faster and more active than other reptiles. With the help of these traits, dinosaurs spread across Earth.
pages.brief: A group of dinosaurs stands upright on land, clearly different from a low crawling reptile nearby. Their large eyes face forward. One dinosaur strides actively across the ground while others spread out across the landscape, showing how these extinct reptiles moved and lived.

pages.text: At least one thousand species of dinosaurs have been discovered and named, but scientists think far more lived on Earth. Dinosaurs could be as small as a chicken or as large as a school bus. Some grew as long as 39 meters (128 ft.). Everything we know about dinosaurs and their world comes from fossils. A fossil is the remains or print of a plant or animal that was preserved in soil or rock. Scientists have found parts of preserved dinosaur skeletons. They have found only a few whole dinosaur skeletons.
pages.brief: A very small dinosaur stands near a huge one, showing the range in size. Nearby, a scientist examines a fossil skeleton preserved in rock. The skeleton is incomplete, pieced from preserved bones, while other fossil remains lie embedded in the surrounding stone.

pages.text: Most of the dinosaur skeletons in museums were put together from parts of many different skeletons. Scientists have also found fossil dinosaur footprints, eggs, and even the contents of dinosaurs’ stomachs. All these things help scientists learn how dinosaurs lived, ate, and died.
pages.brief: In a museum hall, a dinosaur skeleton stands assembled from bones of several different skeletons. Nearby, fossil footprints, eggs, and the preserved contents of a dinosaur’s stomach are displayed as clues. Together they help reveal how dinosaurs lived, ate, and died.

pages.text: A Few Kinds of Dinosaurs Different kinds of dinosaurs lived in different places and at different times. A Tyrannosaurus (ty-ran-uh-SOR-uhs) could never have attacked an Apatosaurus (uh-pa-tuh-SOR-uhs). They lived more than fifty million years apart! Scientists name dinosaurs based on what they looked like and what they ate. Because of this, similar dinosaurs are sorted into larger groups.
pages.brief: Two dinosaurs from different eras appear separated by a wide stretch of time: a Tyrannosaurus and an Apatosaurus never meet. Around them, several other dinosaurs are sorted into larger groups by body shape and diet, showing that different kinds lived in different places and times.

pages.text: Theropods This group of dinosaurs is made up of the scary meat eaters we see so often in movies. One of the largest theropods (THEER-uh-podz), Tyrannosaurus, was up to 6 meters (20 ft.) tall. Another type of theropod was only about the size of a human second grader but ran as fast as a horse.
pages.brief: A towering Tyrannosaurus, a giant meat-eating theropod, stands over a prehistoric plain. Nearby, a much smaller theropod, about the size of a young child, runs swiftly across the ground. Both have two legs and heavy heads, showing the wide size range within this group.

pages.text: Theropods ran on two legs, and they had big, heavy heads and jaws. A Tyrannosaurus tooth could be as long as a dinner plate. Most dinosaurs in this group had giant hooked claws on their feet to catch and kill their food. They were fierce, and fossil skulls show that they also had large brains, which means they were smart. Scientists think they may have lived in family groups and gently cared for their young.
pages.brief: A theropod runs on two legs, its big heavy head and jaws forward. One huge tooth is shown beside a dinner plate for scale, and giant hooked claws grip the ground. Nearby, adult theropods stay close to their young in a family group, caring for the small dinosaurs.

pages.text: Sauropods This next group of dinosaurs included perhaps the largest creatures that ever walked on land. Sauropods (SOR-uh- podz) had large, heavy bodies, legs like tree trunks, and long, slim necks and tails. One type of sauropod may have been as tall as a five-story building. If another type stood on a baseball field, it could stretch from home plate to second base from head to tail.
pages.brief: A huge sauropod stands on land, its heavy body supported by legs like tree trunks. A long slim neck reaches high, while a long tail stretches behind. Nearby, another sauropod is shown stretching across a baseball field from home plate toward second base.

pages.text: Most meat eaters wouldn’t attack a group of these giants. Scientists think that some sauropods may have used their tails as deadly whips. For these dinosaurs, getting enough food was a much bigger problem than staying safe from predators.
pages.brief: A group of giant sauropods stands together, their long necks raised and tails swinging. One sweeps its tail like a deadly whip toward a distant meat eater. Despite the predator, the herd’s biggest struggle is finding enough food to feed their enormous bodies.

pages.text: Ceratopsians The members of this next group of plant eaters were smaller than sauropods. Ceratopsians (sair-uh-TOP-see-uhnz) were usually about 3 to 9 meters (10–30 ft.) long. They made up for their size with large fan-shaped crests that protected their heads and necks. The crests could have as many as fifteen horns.
pages.brief: Several plant-eating ceratopsians gather in a prehistoric landscape. Each has a large fan-shaped crest protecting its head and neck, and some crests bristle with many horns. Smaller than the giant sauropods, these dinosaurs stand about three to nine meters long and browse on low vegetation.

pages.text: Many ceratopsians also had horns on their noses and above their eyes. They had strong parrotlike beaks that could snap tree trunks.
pages.brief: A ceratopsian stands among trees, its strong parrotlike beak biting into a thick trunk. Horns rise from its nose and above its eyes. Another of the same kind watches nearby, its heavy head lowered as it feeds on the tough plants of the prehistoric forest.

pages.text: Pterosaurs While not dinosaurs, this group of animals lived during the same time. Pterosaurs (TAIR-uh-sorz) and dinosaurs are both archosaurs, also known as “ruling reptiles.” Birds and crocodiles fall into this group as well. Aside from insects, pterosaurs were the first animals to ever fly. Most of these flyers ate meat. Some caught fish, lizards, and insects while they flew. Others ate dead animals they came across. Pterosaurs were different sizes. Some were only 25 centimeters (10 in.) long from wing to wing, while others had wings as long as a bus.
pages.brief: A pterosaur glides over water, wings spread wide. Another small pterosaur, only about twenty-five centimeters from wing to wing, flies nearby. One swoops to catch a fish, while another feeds on a dead animal below. These flying reptiles lived during the same time as dinosaurs.

pages.text: The Death of Dinosaurs In time, dinosaurs disappeared from Earth altogether. What happened? Scientists still don’t know for sure. Many think that the crash of an enormous meteorite into Earth was at least partly to blame. The meteorite sent dust and fire into the air. The Sun was blocked out for months. The air became colder. Plants died. Rainwater turned muddy and undrinkable. Both plant eaters and meat eaters could have died from sickness and from not having enough food and water.
pages.brief: A huge meteorite crashes into Earth, throwing dust and fire into the sky. The Sun is blocked out for months, the air turns colder, and plants wither. Rainwater becomes muddy and undrinkable. Dinosaurs stand in the dark, suffering from sickness and a lack of food and water.

pages.text: Whatever killed the dinosaurs also killed hundreds of other kinds of plants and animals. However, one small group of dinosaurs may have survived. When scientists look at the bones of birds and dinosaurs, they see many things in common. Today, many scientists agree that certain types of dinosaurs later became birds. Archaeopteryx.
pages.brief: A small Archaeopteryx stands in a changed prehistoric world. Its bones share many features with both birds and dinosaurs. Around it, many kinds of plants and animals have disappeared. This creature represents the small group of dinosaurs that scientists think may have survived and later become birds.

books.title: Seals, Sea Lions, and Walruses
books.art_why: Seals, sea lions, and walruses are real animals alive today, so photographs fit best.

pages.text: Meet the Pinnipeds You are sitting on a rock by the seashore. Suddenly, a pair of curious eyes peeks up from the water. As quickly as it came, the animal disappears. You are very lucky—you have seen a seal. Seals, along with sea lions and walruses, belong to a group of animals called pinnipeds.
pages.brief: A young person sits on a rock beside the seashore, looking toward the water. A pair of curious seal eyes peeks up from the waves. The seal disappears quickly beneath the surface, leaving the person watching the empty water.

pages.text: Pinnipeds are marine, or ocean, mammals. Mammals are animals that breathe air, have fur, and have live babies that drink their mothers’ milk. Pinnipeds include seals, sea lions, and walruses. Their name comes from a Greek word meaning “fin-footed.” Pinnipeds have flippers instead of feet. Pinnipeds are predators, which means they eat other animals.
pages.brief: A seal, a sea lion, and a walrus swim or float in ocean water, showing flippers instead of feet. Their bodies have fur. One pinniped watches for prey, because pinnipeds are predators that eat other animals.

pages.text: Life in the Ocean Pinnipeds spend most of their lives in the ocean. They have flippers and long, torpedo-shaped bodies to help them swim. These features make pinnipeds graceful in the water, but awkward on land. When a pinniped goes underwater, its nose and throat shut automatically. Some seals can hold their breath for over an hour. Elephant seals can hold it for two!
pages.brief: A pinniped swims gracefully through the ocean with a long, torpedo-shaped body and flippers. Nearby, another pinniped looks awkward on land. Underwater, its nose and throat shut automatically as it holds its breath in deep water.

pages.text: Most pinnipeds eat fish, squid, octopus, and shellfish such as shrimp and clams. Pinnipeds must dive deep to find these animals. The Southern elephant seal can dive over 1,500 meters (5,000 ft)! That is deeper than any other mammal can go. Pinnipeds have large eyes that can see in deep, dark water. They have good ears to hear their prey swimming around. They also have sensitive whiskers that can feel an animal swimming by or moving around on the ocean floor. Depth in meters 1,000 1,250 1,500 1,750 The elephant seal is a champion diver.
pages.brief: A Southern elephant seal dives deep in dark ocean water, its large eyes open and sensitive whiskers alert. Around it swim fish, squid, octopus, shrimp, and clams. The elephant seal hunts prey deeper than any other mammal.

pages.text: Some seals spend their whole lives in and around icy water. Keeping Warm Most pinnipeds live in cold oceans near the North and South Poles. How do pinnipeds keep warm? Many pinnipeds have dense fur with smooth hairs on the top and thick, fluffy hairs on the bottom. The fluffy hairs are waterproof. Pinnipeds also have a layer of fat called blubber that keeps heat inside their bodies. Some pinnipeds have blubber 10 centimeters (4 in) thick.
pages.brief: Pinnipeds swim in cold ocean water near the North and South Poles. One seal shows dense fur with smooth hairs on top and fluffy waterproof hairs underneath. Inside its body, a thick layer of blubber holds heat in.

pages.text: Some pinnipeds do not stay in cold areas for the whole year. They migrate, or move, to warmer water during the winter. Other pinnipeds live in warm areas year round. Warm-water pinnipeds sometimes have trouble keeping cool under their fur and blubber.
pages.brief: Some pinnipeds swim from cold areas toward warmer water for the winter. Others stay in warm areas all year. A warm-water pinniped rests under bright sun, looking uncomfortable under its fur and blubber as it tries to keep cool.

pages.text: Coming to Shore Pinnipeds come to shore, or haul out, to shed their fur, or molt, and to have babies. Some pinnipeds haul out in large groups, while others come to shore one at a time. A pinniped mother has only one baby at a time. The baby, called a pup, can move around and swim as soon as it is born. But it does not have blubber, and it can’t keep warm in water. It usually stays on land. A baby pinniped drinks its mother’s milk for the first few days or weeks of its life. Pinniped milk has lots of fat—it is more like butter than milk. This helps the pup quickly grow a layer of blubber.
pages.brief: A mother pinniped rests on shore beside her single pup, while nearby pinnipeds haul out in a group. Some shed fur. The pup stays on land, without blubber, and drinks rich, fatty milk that helps it grow blubber.

pages.text: Sea Lions Sea lions get their name because some of them have manes and roar like lions. This fur seal looks like a lion. It is called a “seal,” but it belongs in the same group as sea lions. Seals and sea lions look a lot alike. The easiest way to tell them apart is to look for ears. Only sea lions have ears that stick out. Most “trained seals” at ocean parks and aquariums are actually sea lions. Sea lions swim by moving their long necks and long front flippers. They use their back flippers only to steer. Sea lions can also use their flippers to lift their bodies and “walk” on land.
pages.brief: A sea lion with a mane roars like a lion on a rocky shore. Beside it, a fur seal looks similar, but only the sea lion has ears that stick out. The sea lion swims with long neck and front flippers, steers with back flippers, and walks on land.

pages.text: Seals Seals have smaller necks and front flippers than sea lions. They swim by moving their back flippers and hind ends. Seals cannot “walk” on their flippers. Instead, they drag themselves along the ground or crawl like caterpillars.
pages.brief: A seal with a smaller neck and shorter front flippers moves on land. It cannot walk on its flippers, so it drags itself along the ground or crawls like a caterpillar. In the water, it swims by moving its back flippers and hind ends.

pages.text: The biggest pinnipeds in the world are elephant seals. Elephant seals get their name because of their huge size and long noses. Leopard seals are fierce predators. They have big mouths and sharp teeth. They often feed on birds such as penguins. They also attack other seals. Ribbon seals have black fur with white bands. Ringed seals have small, ring-shaped markings.
pages.brief: A huge elephant seal with a long nose rests near a fierce leopard seal that has a big mouth and sharp teeth. The leopard seal watches penguins and other seals. Nearby, a ribbon seal shows black fur with white bands, and a ringed seal has small ring-shaped markings.

pages.text: Do You Know? Walruses Walruses are the only pinnipeds with tusks. They use their tusks to show off to other walruses. They also use them to pull themselves up onto land. Some walruses hook their tusks onto floating ice. Then they relax and sleep.
pages.brief: A walrus with long tusks shows off to another walrus. It uses its tusks to pull itself up onto land. Another walrus hooks its tusks onto floating ice and relaxes, sleeping on the ice.

pages.text: Walruses have very little fur. Their thick skin and blubber keep them warm. When a walrus goes into cold water, its skin turns pale. This is because all of its blood moves to the inside of its body. When the walrus is warm, its blood moves to the surface again. The walrus turns pink. Walruses like to haul out together in big heaps.
pages.brief: A walrus with very little fur hauls out with others in a big heap. Its thick skin and blubber keep it warm. In cold water its skin turns pale as blood moves inside; when warm, blood returns to the surface and the walrus turns pink.

pages.text: People and Pinnipeds People have always hunted pinnipeds. When humans invented large ships and guns, they could hunt and kill many more pinnipeds. Soon, many pinnipeds began dying out. Humans used their fur and skin to make clothing. They ate their meat and burned their blubber as fuel. Only the native people of the far north still hunt pinnipeds. They hunt only what they need to survive.
pages.brief: People hunt pinnipeds from large ships with guns. Hunters use pinniped fur and skin for clothing, eat the meat, and burn blubber as fuel. Native people of the far north still hunt pinnipeds, taking only what they need to survive.

pages.text: People around the world worried about pinnipeds. Countries began making laws against hunting them. Many pinnipeds have begun to come back. But some are still in danger. Pinnipeds become caught in fishing nets. Others get sick because of pollution. Pinnipeds have very few predators, besides humans. It is up to us to decide what their future will be.
pages.brief: People around the world worry about pinnipeds. Countries make laws against hunting them, and many pinnipeds begin to come back. Some remain in danger, caught in fishing nets or sick from pollution. With few predators besides humans, people decide what their future will be.

books.title: The Story of Jeans
books.art_why: The book covers 1800s history and invention, so drawn scenes fit.

pages.text: History Jeans were invented by a German man named Levi Strauss. He went to the U.S. in 1847 and followed the Gold Rush to San Francisco. He carried many kinds of fabric to sell to stores. Business was booming in California during the Gold Rush. Levi quickly became successful. The miners in California had a problem with their pants. When they found gold or ore, they carried it in their pockets. But the metal was heavy, and the pockets ripped. In 1873, Levi became partners with a tailor named Jacob Davis. Jacob and Levi made tough denim pants. They put copper rivets in the seams. Rivets are strong metal fasteners. The miners loved the “waist overalls,” as they were called. The pants quickly became popular.
pages.brief: Levi Strauss, a German man, stands with bolts of fabric in Gold Rush San Francisco, selling to stores. Miners carry heavy gold and ore in pockets that rip. In 1873 Levi and tailor Jacob Davis make tough denim pants with copper rivets in the seams; miners wear the waist overalls.

pages.text: Changing Fashions Levi’s® jeans were work pants. Male workers wore them all the time. But a gentleman wouldn’t think of wearing jeans. Women didn’t wear pants at all. This changed when Western movies became popular. All the cowboys wore jeans. People thought the cowboys looked tough and cool. But jeans still weren’t worn in places like school, stores, or offices. During the second World War, off-duty U.S. soldiers wore jeans. They made jeans seem like tough, casual American pants. They became a symbol of America in many other countries. Today, we call denim pants “jeans.” But jean and denim are two different fabrics. Denim is a strong all-cotton fabric. Jean is a thinner, weaker fabric. It is made of cotton and linen. But both fabrics are dyed blue with indigo. They look very much alike. Many people called Levi’s pants “jeans.” So, the company changed the name. Jean or Denim?
pages.brief: Male workers wear Levi’s jeans as work pants, while a gentleman and women do not wear jeans. Western movies show cowboys looking tough and cool in jeans. Off-duty U.S. soldiers in World War II wear jeans, making them a casual American symbol. Denim and jean fabrics are both dyed blue with indigo.

pages.text: Back in the U.S., fashions changed. Movie stars wore jeans in their films. Teenagers everywhere loved them. Some schools banned jeans. But casual clothing became popular for more occasions. Eventually, it became okay for anyone to wear jeans. You can even find pictures of a president wearing jeans. In the 1980s, new styles of jeans were created. There were bleached, decorated, and worn- out jeans. There were baggy, stretchy, and flared jeans. In 2000, a pair of jeans sold for $3,715.
pages.brief: Back in the U.S., movie stars wear jeans in films and teenagers love them. Some schools ban jeans, but casual clothing becomes popular for more occasions, and even a president wears jeans. In the 1980s, bleached, decorated, worn-out, baggy, stretchy, and flared jeans appear; in 2000 a pair sells for $3,715.

pages.text: Jeans are dyed every color of the rainbow. Denim is used to make many things, such as jackets, hats, skirts, shoes, and wallets. Antique, or old, jeans are also popular. You can find them in thrift stores for a very low price. Or you can find them in specialty stores, where they cost much more. These jeans are a copy of jeans made in the 1880s. Most jeans begin as fibers growing on cotton plants. The fibers are in puffs called bolls. The bolls are picked and the seeds are removed. Then the fibers are combed to untangle them. The fibers are called lint. Machines twist the lint into a thick rope. The rope is pulled, twisted, and stretched into a long, thin thread called yarn. Do You Know? Many blue jeans are sewn with orange thread. This is unusual. Most clothing is sewn with thread the same color as the fabric. The orange thread matches the copper rivets. Many jeans have two stitches side by side to make the orange show up. How Jeans Are Made.
pages.brief: Jeans are dyed every color, and denim makes jackets, hats, skirts, shoes, and wallets. Old antique jeans sit in thrift and specialty stores, some copied from 1880s jeans. Cotton bolls are picked, seeds removed, fibers combed into lint, then machines twist lint into yarn. Orange thread and copper rivets show on many jeans.

pages.text: Making Blue Jeans Blue Jeans can be dyed with indigo. This dye comes from special plants. The plant leaves are first soaked in water. Then the water is stirred to mix in oxygen. This makes the plant mixture blue. But indigo is very expensive. For many years, jeans makers used dye from coal or oil. But these dyes cause pollution. Some jeans makers have found special bacteria that make blue dye. The next pair of blue jeans you buy may have been dyed by bacteria! Bundles of fabric are called bolts. One bolt of denim weighs 500 pounds (227 kg). It can make 60 pairs of adult-size jeans. Electric saws cut through 120 layers of cloth at once. The cloth is cut into many sizes and sewn together. One pair of jeans goes through 37 sewing steps. It takes 213 yards (195 m) of thread to sew one pair of jeans. Yarn is dyed before it is woven into denim. Blue denim is made from blue and white yarn. When jeans wear out or rip, you can see the white threads. Denim is woven in a diagonal pattern. The fabric is so strong that it is used in some paper money. That’s why paper money doesn’t fall apart if it gets wet.
pages.brief: Blue jeans are dyed with indigo from plant leaves soaked and stirred in water, or with dyes from coal or oil; some bacteria make blue dye. A 500-pound bolt of denim can make 60 pairs. Electric saws cut 120 layers, and one pair goes through 37 sewing steps with 213 yards of thread.

pages.text: Round bobbins pull and twist lint into yarn. 3 The fabric is cut into patterns and sizes. 4 The cut fabric is sewn together to make jeans. 2 Looms weave the yarn into strips of cloth. Now, people can order custom-made jeans. You can send your measurements to a custom jeans company. They will make a pair to fit you perfectly.
pages.brief: Round bobbins pull and twist lint into yarn, and looms weave the yarn into strips of cloth. The fabric is cut into patterns and sizes, then the cut fabric is sewn together to make jeans. Now people can order custom-made jeans by sending measurements to a company for a perfect fit.

pages.text: Conclusion Today, all kinds of people around the world wear jeans. People wear them everywhere. Designers have even made denim suits for formal events. Jeans are popular today for the same reasons they were popular when Levi Strauss first made them. They look good, they last long, and they are comfortable. custom (adj.) page 16 made specifically for one person rivets (n.) page 6 bits of metal that hold things together casual (adj.) page 8 relaxed; not formal ore (n.) page 6 rock with precious metal in it bolts (n.) page 14 wide, rolled-up strips of fabric linen (n.) page 8 a thin, light fabric made from a plant called flax bolls (n.) page 12 puffs of cotton indigo (n.) page 8 a dye made from plants; also, a deep, dark blue color diagonal (adj.) page 14 slanted; at an angle antique (adj.) page 11 valuable and old Glossary.
pages.brief: All kinds of people around the world wear jeans everywhere, and designers have made denim suits for formal events. Jeans are popular for the same reasons as when Levi Strauss first made them: they look good, last long, and are comfortable.

books.title: About Trees
books.art_why: Trees and their parts are real natural subjects that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Introduction Trees are the tallest living plants. Redwood trees can grow as tall as a 30-story building. Giant sequoias can weigh as much as 3,000 large pickup trucks, making them one of the heaviest living things. Trees also live a long time. Many trees alive today were full-grown long before the United States became a country. But these massive trees share something with all plants—they make their own food.
pages.brief: A towering redwood forest, with one redwood rising beside a thirty-story building for scale, and a giant sequoia with an enormous trunk. Around them stand old, full-grown trees. Sunlight falls on green needles and leaves as the trees make their own food.

pages.text: Leaves Imagine being able to make your own food without cooking or even going to a restaurant! Leaves make food for trees by changing energy from sunlight into food. This important work is done by chlorophyll (KLOR-uh-fill), the green coloring in leaves. Leaves come in all shapes and sizes. Most deciduous (dee-SIJ-oo-us) trees have wide, thin leaves, while most conifers have needlelike leaves. Conifers keep their needles through all seasons. Only the oldest needles fall to the ground. Deciduous trees lose their leaves every fall.
pages.brief: A close-up of broad, thin deciduous leaves and narrow conifer needles on nearby branches, both lit by bright sunlight. The green leaves and needles show the green coloring that helps make food. A deciduous tree has wide leaves, while a conifer keeps its needlelike leaves through the seasons.

pages.text: In the fall, the leaves of deciduous trees show their true colors. These true colors are yellows, oranges, and browns, which hide under green chlorophyll all spring and summer. We see these colors in the fall after leaves stop making chlorophyll.
pages.brief: A deciduous tree in autumn, its leaves glowing yellow, orange, and brown. A close view shows the same colors in the leaves where green has faded. The tree stands under soft fall sunlight, with some leaves still on branches and some fallen on the ground.

pages.text: Branches Branches are the arms that hold up a tree’s leaves. Branches spread leaves out to get as much sunlight as they can. The leaves give shade to other living things on sunny days. Branches start out as twigs, then they grow thicker each year. As a tree grows, its bark cracks open so the branches and trunk can expand. New bark is always growing under the old, ready to protect the tree. If new bark gets stripped away, a tree can die.
pages.brief: A tree with spreading branches reaching out and holding many leaves toward the sunlight. Below, the leaves cast shade on the ground and on small living things. A close view of a branch shows twigs growing thicker and bark cracking open as new bark forms underneath.

pages.text: Trunk Tubes in the tree’s trunk carry water from the roots up to the leaves. They also carry sap, or food, down from the leaves to the roots. These tubes are like highways, carrying traffic back and forth. They are close to the outside of the tree, just under the bark.
pages.brief: A tree trunk shown in cutaway, with narrow tubes just under the bark running from the roots up toward the leaves and back down. The tubes carry water upward and sap downward, like busy highways inside the trunk. The trunk stands tall, with roots below and leafy branches above.

pages.text: A tree doesn’t need the middle of its trunk to live. The middle is made of rings of old growth, not active highways. That’s why a tree can keep growing even if the middle is hollowed out after a lightning strike. All it needs is enough bark to protect its highways.
pages.brief: An old tree trunk with a hollow middle, opened by a lightning strike. Rings of old growth fill the center, while healthy bark remains around the outside. The tree still stands and grows, with leaves above and roots below, protected by enough bark to keep its inner tubes safe.

pages.text: Roots Trees need soil to keep growing. Roots are part of the highways. They soak up water and nutrients from the soil. Roots also keep the soil in place when it rains. Without the roots of trees and plants, soil washes away. Trees are stuck in the soil because their roots reach deep into the ground. It’s a good thing they can make their own food, since they can’t move to get it.
pages.brief: A tree rooted deep in dark soil, with roots spreading through the ground. Rain falls, and the roots hold the soil in place so it does not wash away. The tree stands fixed in the earth, soaking up water and nutrients while its leafy top reaches upward.

pages.text: Sap Leaves use water plus sunlight and air to make food for the tree. This food is in the form of liquid sugars. Sometimes people eat some kinds of tree sugars for food. You’ve probably had tree sugar for breakfast—pouring it over your pancakes or waffles. Have you guessed what tree sugar this is? It’s maple syrup, and it comes from the food, or sap, of a sugar maple tree.
pages.brief: A sugar maple tree with its sap shown as liquid sugar inside the trunk and leaves. A bottle of maple syrup stands beside pancakes and waffles, with syrup being poured over them. Sunlight falls on the maple leaves that help make the tree’s food.

pages.text: Seeds Deciduous trees grow flowers, which make seeds that are inside fruit or nuts. Conifers make cones instead of flowers. The cones do the same job for conifers that flowers do on other trees. They make seeds to grow more trees. Each seed holds its own supply of food to keep it alive until it’s ready to sprout.
pages.brief: A deciduous tree with flowers that become fruit and nuts holding seeds. Nearby, a conifer holds cones instead of flowers. Close views show seeds inside fruit, nuts, and cones, each seed carrying its own small supply of food.

pages.text: Growing How does a tall tree grow from a small seed? The seed soaks up water until it can send out a root. With more water, leaves inside the seed case grow until they push up and out. Once this has happened, we say the seed has sprouted. Now the sprout can make its own food and no longer needs the seed’s store of energy. The seed leaves will make food for the new sprout.
pages.brief: A small seed in wet soil, soaking up water and sending out a first root. Inside the seed case, tiny leaves grow until they push up and out of the soil. The sprouted seed now has seed leaves that make food for the new sprout.

pages.text: Conclusion While trees look like they aren’t doing much, they are working. They make their own food by changing sunlight and air into sugars. This helps keep the air clean, too. Trees are homes and food for birds and other animals. Look to see which animals make homes in trees near your home. Some animals, including humans, eat sap, fruit, and seeds from trees. Others eat bark and leaves.
pages.brief: A broad tree full of leaves, with birds nesting in its branches and eating fruit and seeds. A person eats sap, fruit, or seeds from a tree, while another animal eats bark and leaves. Sunlight falls on the tree as its leaves make sugars and help keep the air clean.

pages.text: Trees do many things. Tree leaves shade us on sunny days. They also shade new sprouts from the heat of the sun so they won’t burn. Tree roots hold the soil in place that trees and other plants need to grow. From saplings to mighty giants, trees stand tall.
pages.brief: A tall tree with leafy branches casting shade on a person below and on a small new sprout. Its roots spread through the soil, holding the ground in place. Nearby, a young sapling stands beside a mighty giant tree, showing trees from small to tall.

books.title: Deep Inside a Copper Mine
books.art_why: The Queen Mine Tour in Bisbee, Arizona, is a real modern place that exists today.

pages.text: Deep Inside a Copper Mine.
pages.brief: A wide view of the Queen Mine tour site in Bisbee, Arizona, showing the mine entrance and the tour building under a bright sky. The outdoor scene sets up a visit to an old copper mine.

pages.text: The Queen Mine Tour parking lot sat virtually empty at 1:30 pm on a hot March day. Mom, Sam, and I were going on a tour of the old Bisbee, Arizona, copper mine at 2 pm. My favorite blue sweatshirt was tied around my waist. Mom said the mine was like Grandma’s house in Tennessee. Not too cold, but not warm. That translated into cool for me. On the tour, I learned that the mine stays at about 47 degrees Fahrenheit. Actually, that is downright cold to me.
pages.brief: A nearly empty parking lot outside the Queen Mine Tour building in Bisbee, Arizona, on a hot March afternoon. Mom, Sam, and the narrator stand together, the narrator with a blue sweatshirt tied around the waist, about to join the 2 pm tour.

pages.text: I imagined walking through the front door of the Queen Mine Tour building and seeing a humongous gaping hole in a rock wall. Instead, I saw counters and shelves of gear on my right—yellow rain slickers, hardhats, and belt-looking things with lamps. There was an old fireplace spewing heat even though it was hot as the dickens outside. The room even smelled like Grandma’s house. Mom was more right than she thought.
pages.brief: Inside the Queen Mine Tour building, the narrator sees counters and shelves of gear: yellow rain slickers, hardhats, and belts with lamps. An old fireplace gives off heat. Mom stands nearby in the warm room.

pages.text: What I didn’t realize was that the rain slickers were for us. We had to put them on before going into the mine. I hated the whole idea of putting on a heavy vinyl coat that hardly let you breathe. First, I put on my sweatshirt, then the yellow slicker. It was stiff and made crackly sounds as I shoved my arms through the clammy holes.
pages.brief: The narrator pulls on a stiff yellow vinyl rain slicker over a blue sweatshirt, arms pushing through clammy holes. Mom and Sam are nearby getting ready. The heavy coat crackles as the group prepares to enter the mine.

pages.text: I immediately felt a weight around my waist as the tour guide placed a battery pack around me. He showed me how to clip a lamp to my rain slicker; then, I heard it snap closed. The best part was that I got to wear a hardhat. It almost made the yucky, stiff feeling of the slicker worth the trip.
pages.brief: A tour guide places a battery pack around the narrator's waist and clips a lamp onto the yellow rain slicker. The narrator wears a hardhat. The guide shows how the gear works inside the tour building.

pages.text: We walked through the building and out the back door to the outside. The sunlight hurt my eyes and made me see stars. My sweatshirt and slicker weighed more than I thought they would. We climbed on board what the tour guide called a man-car. All of the sudden this was getting to be fun. Everyone had to straddle these padded benches in the center of each car like we were riding on the back of one long horse. The guide started up the engine, which sounded like a big lawn mower, and the man-car chugged toward the mine.
pages.brief: Outside the tour building, the narrator and others climb onto a man-car with padded benches. Everyone straddles the benches like riding a long horse. The guide starts the engine, which sounds like a lawn mower, and the car moves toward the mine.

pages.text: We got about 100 feet into the mine when the tour guide stopped. He said that if anyone felt claustrophobic, they could get off and walk back. Mom explained to me that some people are scared of tight places. I have to admit, the tunnel was pretty narrow and stuffy. No one turned back though.
pages.brief: About 100 feet inside the mine, the man-car stops in a narrow, stuffy tunnel. The tour guide speaks to the group. Mom leans toward the narrator. No one gets off to walk back.

pages.text: The clang, clang of metal wheels on metal tracks made a racket in the tunnel. The man-car vibrated as the angle going down got steeper. The lamps we clipped to our slickers soon became the only lights in the mine. The man-car stopped on the third floor down. We got off and walked through a side tunnel. This tunnel was wide enough to fit about three people across.
pages.brief: The man-car rolls down a steep tunnel, metal wheels clanging on metal tracks. The lamps on the slickers are the only light. The car stops on the third floor down, and the group walks through a side tunnel wide enough for three people across.

pages.text: The air in the mine smelled and tasted funny. It was like I was breathing bits of the copper. It made my teeth hurt. The air was damp, too. Small patches of mud dotted the dirt floor. I could see why we needed the slickers as water drops fell from the rock above us.
pages.brief: Inside the mine, the narrator walks through a tunnel where the air smells and tastes like copper. Small patches of mud dot the dirt floor, and water drops fall from the rock above. The narrator wears the yellow slicker and hardhat.

pages.text: The guide told us stories about his work in the mine. He showed us a cage, which is an elevator with wire mesh instead of walls. He said it took miners all the way down to the bottom of the mine. They would cram the elevator full of miners and then go down. Miners really couldn’t be claustrophobic and keep their jobs.
pages.brief: The tour guide stands with the group and points out a cage, an elevator with wire mesh instead of walls. He tells stories about miners cramming into it to ride to the bottom of the mine. The narrator listens in the tunnel.

pages.text: The guide showed us some holes in the wall. Miners filled the holes with sticks of dynamite and wired them to blow up the rock. The miners would blast the rock at the end of their shift. After a blast, the air would be thick with dust, making the air heavy and hard to breathe.
pages.brief: The guide shows the group holes in the mine wall. He explains how miners filled the holes with dynamite and wired them to blast the rock at the end of a shift. The narrator looks at the holes in the rock.

pages.text: We went to another part of the mine before we headed back to the top. This part was a big room with lots of little cubbyholes. The tour guide asked us to shine our lights on different parts of the room. I couldn’t believe it! Every now and then, a light would glance off something with a dull shine. He said that was malachite, a beautiful green mineral often found with copper ore.
pages.brief: In a big room with many little cubbyholes, the tour guide asks everyone to shine their lamps on different parts of the rock. A dull green shine reveals malachite, a green mineral found with copper ore. The narrator aims a lamp.

pages.text: At one point in our tour, the guide had us all turn off our lamps. Oh, my gosh, it was so dark. I had never been in total darkness before. There was absolutely no light. I held my hand right in front of my face and I couldn’t even see it. Just as I was beginning to feel scared, the guide had us turn our lamps back on. Do You Know? The Queen Mine produced 8 billion pounds of copper in its 100 years of operation. The copper came from copper ore, which needs to be smelted before the metal in the rock can be used. Also produced by the Queen Mine were: • 2.8 million ounces of gold • 77 million pounds of silver • 30 million pounds of lead • 371 million pounds of zinc.
pages.brief: In total darkness inside the mine, the narrator holds a hand in front of their face but cannot see it. The tour guide has everyone turn off their lamps. The group stands still in the dark before the lamps come back on.

pages.text: When we got back to the top and the tour was done, I was happy to feel the sunshine. I couldn’t wait to get out of the slicker, heavy belt, and hardhat. I ditched the gear where the guide said to, then ran to the fire to warm up. I couldn’t believe I was so cold, but I was. Though it was later than when we arrived, it was still a hot 90 degrees outside, and that felt warm against my cold skin. Though I had enjoyed the trip through the mine, I had to admit that being a miner was not the job for me. Everyone leaves to go home.
pages.brief: Back at the surface, the narrator removes the slicker, heavy belt, and hardhat and runs to a fire to warm up. The sun shines outside at 90 degrees. Other visitors leave the Queen Mine Tour building to go home.
